#974. Los Angeles Golf Club make history by winning inaugural WTGL match

The inaugural WTGL season teed off at SoFi Center in Florida with Los Angeles Golf Club defeating New York Golf Club; the opener included walk-up videos from the parking lot, flashy intros for the fans on hand, some funky fashion and Serena Williams in attendance

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Los Angeles Golf Club sealed a 3-1 victory over New York in an historic first WTGL match at SoFi Center.

Lydia Ko and Michelle Wie West were among the six players in action who treated an audience of 1,500 fans at the indoor venue in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida to some spectacular shot-making, several dramatic near-misses and pure entertainment between the mic'd-up players.

Wie West, Alison Lee and Gaby Lopez eventually out-duelled Rose Zhang and her team-mates in Linn Grant and Ko.

New York's Zhang broke new ground as she hit the first tee shot, one that she blasted 301 yards into the fairway on Cut The Sails.

Wie West came agonisingly close to registering a hole-in-in-one at the par-three seventh as Los Angeles built a narrow 2-1 lead over New York after the first nine holes of team play. New York took number 5, and Lee took down Grant on number 11

In the closing holes, New York had chances, but Zhang missed two short putts on the 13th hole and Grant missed a 10-foot putt on the 14th.

That secured the win for Los Angeles, 3-1, before the teams tied the final hole.

"Our purses are growing up, and we get to play the most amazing golf courses we've ever played," Lee said. "For people to experience and see us play in a different setting, in a more intimate and personal setting, is very different, and hopefully it can bring more eyeballs to the game."

Los Angeles will have a chance to build a verifiable winning streak on Tuesday as the inaugural season begins to ramp up.

Wie West and co will take on Motor City Golf Club, who boast a line-up led by Lexi Thompson and Brooke Henderson.

The WTGL follows on from the success of the Tomorrow's Golf League (TGL), founded by Tiger Woods and Rory McIlroy's TMRW Sports, in partnership with the PGA Tour.

The women's edition of the tech-infused golf league will see LPGA Tour stars feature in a unique team format, with five teams (representing five different cities) of five-player rosters confirmed for the inaugural season.

The season-long competition takes place across November and December at the SoFi Center in Florida, a purpose-built indoor venue, with every shot live and all the players mic'd up for the made-for-TV format.

Both the 2026 and 2027 editions of WTGL will be broadcast exclusively on Sky Sports as part of an expansion of its golf rights, which also includes a further two years of TGL presented by SoFi.

Every match will be exclusively live on Sky Sports Golf, Sky Sports+ or Sky Sports Mix, while repeats will be available the following day on Sky Sports Golf. You can also download the Sky Sports App for news, highlights, scores and reports.

#973. Billions in revenue proves Fifa right on the World Cup – but only on things it cares about

The 2026 edition of the tournament brought in untold amounts of money to Gianni Infantino’s governing body

The total hasn’t entirely stopped rising yet, still clicking away towards a final tally. Still, Fifa has already announced that it surpassed its own lofty revenue projections for the 2026 World Cup, bringing in $15bn, significantly more than anticipated. It appears that a third of that total – $5bn – came from ticket sales and hospitality alone, per reporting from the Times.

That would mean direct income from the matchgoing fans came in five times as high in the United States, Canada and Mexico as it did at the last World Cup, in Qatar in 2022, when the total stood at $929m. While 2026’s expanded World Cup added 40 games to the schedule, the takings nevertheless went from an average of about $14.5m per match to about $48m.

Which is to say that Fifa, and by extension its all-controlling president Gianni Infantino, was right.

Wrong, mind you, about what it believes anybody with a modicum of taste would think is cool and enjoyable. Like putting Robbie Williams in everything; or cramming Madonna, and BTS, and Shakira, and Justin Bieber, and Ted Lasso, and the Muppets into a World Cup final half-time show that catered to the appetites of the lobotomized; or setting up a pre-final speech on greatness by Tom Cruise.

Wrong, too, about mandatory hydration breaks, and suspending red cards, and stretching the aforementioned, accursed half-time show to 27 minutes in violation of Fifa’s own rules.

But right about all the things Fifa cares about. Which can be neatly reduced to money.

Right that exposing ticket sales – and even parking – to dynamic pricing, driving their prices far out of reach of your average fan, would pay off. Right that it could annex the secondary ticket market and take a hefty cut of resales. Right that the PR hit of cozying up to Donald Trump – who was already deeply unpopular, especially among America’s left-leaning soccer crowd – would not be mortal and, in fact, would not even cost Fifa any money at all. That tolerating the excesses of the Trump government – the disgraceful treatment of the Iranian team, its bluster about potential ICE action around stadiums and its denial of visas to fans and journalists hoping to attend the tournament – would be worth it in order to safeguard the money gusher. (These things may all yet be investigated, among about a million other things, but Fifa’s money is made all the same.)

Right, in the end, that the World Cup is too big to fail. That the decadence and cravenness of the World Cup’s organizers will, in the end, be redeemed by the tournament itself. That the World Cup is unfuckupable.

As things stand, it looks like Infantino may very well survive the fallout of his foolhardy and utterly tone-deaf attempt to quickly and unilaterally sell a chunk of the World Cup’s commercial rights to private equity. That was a bridge too far even in the world’s most cynical sport, but the tournament’s profits appear to have consolidated his power in spite of it all. Infantino has an election to get through in March, but a great many of his ardent supporters are apparently unmoved by the scandal and stand resolutely behind him. While he can’t quite do whatever he wants, it appears he also can’t commit an act grievous enough to be dislodged from power.

As Fifa pointed out to the Athletic, the World Cup’s attendance of 6.8 million was unprecedented – the previous record, from the 1994 World Cup in the United States, was just under 3.6 million. And hat means bigger payouts for Fifa’s 211 member associations, each of which has a presidential-election vote.

This, and only this, is why there is no reforming Fifa until the money stream is somehow slowed. The real power in soccer lies with the money – everything and everyone else is just a figurehead. The sport is organized and optimized to facilitate only the flow of money. We were reminded of this same truth just last week when comments emerged of Kylian Mbappé making light of a meme involving himself and China’s former leader Mao Zedong. The Real Madrid star quickly lost several endorsement deals in China, and scurried to apologize faster than he’s ever loped after a through ball.

Infantino understands this innately and behaves accordingly. And for all his blundering behavior, for all the ugliness and moral insolvency of his grubby masterpiece, the final takeaway from the 2026 World Cup is that, actually, this is all fine. It worked. Pandering to politicians? Proof, meet pudding. The money poured in at an unprecedented flow rate, a rapids of revenue. So, you know, carry on.

And that, to use a term from these lands that have made Fifa even wealthier, sucks.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

#972. ‘Mathematics is more than a mechanical process’ — why I think the field will survive OpenAI’s disruption

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Ursula Martin is an emeritus professor at the Mathematical Institute, University of Oxford, UK.

In early October, the artificial-intelligence firm OpenAI posted more than 700 AI-generated mathematical manuscripts on an online public repository. The arguments — if found to be correct after verification — contain an extraordinary trove of new mathematical knowledge. The reaction to these developments from the maths community has ranged from exhilaration to despair. Some researchers worry they have spent their lifetimes attempting to solve problems and their work might now suddenly seem meaningless. Others have expressed concern about the negative impact on young colleagues who are entering the field during a period of flux. And there’s been widespread anger at the manner in which AI companies are releasing such findings.

As one of the authors of the Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics, which was published in June, I think some of the field’s concerns over OpenAI’s approach to announcing its discoveries could have been anticipated. In our declaration, we did not oppose the use of AI but put forwards several practical safeguards. These included the need for clear citation policies, precise disclosures on how AI is used and a renewed commitment to the long-standing expectation that all arguments made in a maths proof should be independently verifiable and answerable by a human author. Some AI companies have agreed to follow the declaration. OpenAI has not.

Mathematicians are developing rules for AI use — other fields should follow

Mathematicians are developing rules for AI use — other fields should follow

Now that mathematicians have started analysing the AI-assisted proofs, it’s clear that many of the 700 preprints are presented in a sloppy, rough-and-ready style, making them hard to understand. The inner workings of OpenAI’s closed models are unknown, and there is also no human author named who might take responsibility for explaining or correcting the content if flaws emerge. It will take mathematicians a lot of time and effort to check the work in the preprints and rewrite it in a professional format that is suitable for judgement by peer reviewers. Unsurprisingly, many mathematicians are unenthusiastic about clearing up OpenAI’s mess, however exciting the underlying mathematics might be.

So, what does this mean for the future of mathematics? Creatively rethinking how the field must evolve will require action at every level. Outstanding leadership by individuals such as mathematician Terence Tao, and grassroots initiatives such as the Leiden declaration, need to be complemented with high-level engagement from stakeholder institutions such as the International Mathematical Union. It would be a disservice to the field if AI companies are allowed to set the norms on how to do mathematics without wide-ranging input from academics.

#970. Folarin Balogun takes a first, tiny step toward moving on from a calamitous summer

The USMNT striker scored his first goal since the World Cup in a losing effort against Paris FC. Could it lead to something more?

Before this weekend, the last time Folarin Balogun scored was in the United States’ 2-0 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina at this past summer’s World Cup. In the immediate aftermath, the outlook for Balogun seemed rosy; an ascendant player who could muster a goal in tense games. At half-time against Bosnia, US fans weren’t just wondering how far his team could advance – they were sizing Balogun up against some of the world’s best strikers.

But for most of the ensuing four months, Balogun has been in limbo. His breakout World Cup was overshadowed by a red card in that same game against Bosnia and Herzegovina, followed by a scandal of which he wanted no part. Just as it seemed a summer move away from Monaco could get his club career on track, he broke off a possible deadline-day move to Everton after a lengthy visit to the training grounds and a medical he felt was improperly handled.

While many expect that Balogun will get his move in January, to the Premier League or elsewhere, Monaco have understandably prepared for life without him. New manager Filipe Luís continues to prefer 20-year-old German youth international Paris Brunner to Balogun, giving the youngster ample time to tap into his vast potential. Balogun’s opportunities to turn the page have been limited.

On Sunday, though, Balogun took the first steps toward a brighter future, scoring the lone goal as Monaco fell 3-1 to Paris FC.

Monaco struggled to muster any meaningful chances in the first half against Paris, with Brunner sending the team’s only shot wide. Paris FC attacked relentlessly, stunning the early Ligue 1 title hopefuls with two goals just before half-time.

On days when Brunner puts it all together, such as when he bagged a brace against Marseille, he lives up to Luis’s faith. On other days, like Sunday, that faith can backfire. Enter Balogun.

Luís gave the American a chance to buck his months-long drought, bringing him on at half-time in place of Brunner, with a golden opportunity presenting itself in the 66th minute. Monaco broke up the right flank with a dribble from Brazilian right-back Vanderson, with Balogun running the channels while the Paris defense backtracked. Vanderson played a teasing low cross into the mixer that the goalkeeper couldn’t claim. Balogun needed just one prod, directing the ball to the far post. It wasn’t pretty, but it looked exceedingly comfortable, a rare return to the happy place that Balogun once frequented.

Just last season, Balogun finished fourth in Ligue 1’s goalscoring charts, bagging 13 for Monaco, with another six in the Champions League and the Coupe de France. His good form continued at the World Cup, with two first-half goals in the opening rout of Paraguay. His movement forced Australia into an own goal, with the Bosnia game providing him a third goal. Even in the expanded 48-team field in a particularly goal-saturated World Cup, only 10 players outscored him.

All of which only makes what came next even more complicated. Speaking with the media two days after the Bosnia game, Balogun called the entire red-card saga “surreal”, but refused to play victim. His message focused on making sure the next generation saw, through him, “the correct way to handle things, even when you think it’s unjust.” You really got the sense he wanted to move on from the whole episode.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Instead, Balogun has become an unwilling avatar in football fans’ suspicion of how football is run, one of the first names cited whenever Gianni Infantino is skewered for other controversial acts. He seems to have gotten grace for pulling the plug on joining David Moyes’s side, a sequence largely dismissed as “LOL Everton” fodder rather than an indictment of the player. But nonetheless, Balogun’s current standing at Monaco will hardly keep him operating at the requisite level to be a crucial player for Mauricio Pochettino. Luis also omitted Balogun from Monaco’s squad for the Uefa Conference League, limiting his participation to domestic competitions – where the manager has preferred Brunner.

A goal in a losing effort does not reverse any of this. But it may be the first step in Balogun’s quest to move past the events of the last few months – a timely reminder that with good service and a manager’s faith, he could still be a high-level scoring option. His time coming through Arsenal’s academy makes him a valuable prospect for Premier League suitors, nursing their homegrown player quotas for domestic and continental competition. Manchester United are reportedly one possibility, in case wants even more anxiety in his life; Juventus may be another.

More than goals, though, increased minutes would do wonders to help Balogun move on from a summer that’s redefined his reputation. While he still projects to be a rung above national team newcomers Julian Hall and Justin Ellis, the pair are starting games in MLS and scoring with regularity. It’s first-choice status that Balogun is yearning to hold once again.

#967. 'I persuaded my club to give me a job as a content creator'

If someone would've said to me I'd be doing this as a job when I was 12, I wouldn't have believed them.

My name's Jacob. I'm a content creator, and I work with Bolton Wanderers.

My role here at Bolton is coming up with new ideas for social media, to try new concepts, filming stuff, and then posting them onto Bolton's pages and trying to help people follow the club. In my opinion, I think it's one of the funnest jobs in football, and it's brilliant.

Right. Welcome to Bolton, Larra. I hope I said that right. I'm going to teach you some Bolton twang to help you settle in.

My passion for football when I was growing up started at a very young age. My dad used to take me to the football matches, and I got my very first season ticket when I was five years old in the 2010/11 season, when Bolton was in the Premiership. Being something I loved as a kid, to turn it into my job is amazing.

I work here at least two days a week, obviously filming content, producing content,and then on match day, I'll be filming mostly with fans, and I love it.

As a town? Well, for us, it's lovely. Yeah.

Mondays, meetings. We have the marketing meeting, so that gives you an idea of what the week holds, what I'm going to do on a match day with the fans. And then in the week, I either film in with players, retail, commercial,whatever department needs help producing videos.

Some of the skills I use, I think one of them's got to be communication. You've got to be able to talk to people, talk to fans, and if you're watching this and you're a bit shy, or you think you can't communicate with people as well, I was like that inhigh school, so you learn it as you get older. But working in football, you've got to be adaptable because one minute you're doing a new signing, next minute you're working with the players, next minute it's a match day, next minute the season's over.

I'd say another one is being creative. That's probably the most important one because without being creative, you won't be able to put a video together.

So when I was 16 in high school, that's where my journey started. I did videos, which got me a number of followers. I always struggled in the classroom side in high school, but creating content and creating ideas and being creative, I was always really, really good at in high school, whether that would be doing something drama-related or English, writing, creating stories. I always knew I had a passion for creative pieces of work and being able to now do it as a job, it suits me down to the ground.

I didn't go to college. I didn't go to uni. I left high school with no GCSEs, but I've always had a real passion for football, so that's how I got in contact with Bolton Wanderers. I started doing some videos here at Bolton with the fans and that, and then it turned into going to the training ground and filming with the players, working with the commercial team, retail team, all the different departmentsaround the football club to eventually getting a paid role in football.

I think don't wait for an opportunity to come to you. Get out there and try. If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role there. But if it doesn't, then you've also created a portfolio working with different people, different businesses, different companies, and it's really good for your CV and for future opportunities with different companies.

The highlight of my career so far, probably looking back, being resilient enough to create my own career path in doing something I love.

When you score this season, you might be chuffed.

If you're passionate about football, you're a bit creative, and you're good in front of the camera, content creation infootball might be a job for you.

To find out what other careers you can have in football, explore the BBC Bitesize Follow Your Passion collection.

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

He's a content creator for Bolton Wanderers FC, coming up with new ideas for social media, filming videos and posting them onto official pages. The aim is to encourage people to follow the club.

There are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he says. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities."

Jacob says salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

Find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

This information is a guide and is constantly changing. Please check the National Careers Service website for the latest information and all the qualifications needed and the GOV.UK website for more on T-levels.

#966. From VHS dreams to San Siro glory: Amorim’s Milan surge puts rivals on notice | Nicky Bandini

Inspired by the legendary Milan sides of his youth, the manager gave his side a lift with a tactical victory over Inter

Ruben Amorim had waited a lifetime for his first Milan derby. As a kid growing up in Lisbon, he supported two football teams. There was the local one, Benfica, whose games he attended so early in life that his father has recalled changing nappies in the stands of the old Estádio da Luz. And the other one that captivated him from overseas.

“I remember watching tapes of that Milan team with [Paolo] Maldini, [Franco] Baresi, [Ruud] Gullit, [Frank] Rijkaard, [Dejan] Savicevic,” Amorim told the Portuguese newspaper Expresso in 2017. “My childhood dreams were to play for Benfica and Milan. I’ve fulfilled one. Now I suppose I’ll have to become a coach for the other!”

It took him another nine years to achieve that ambition. The Milan side he inherited in June did not look like the continental conquerors he used to admire on VHS. This version had just missed out on the Champions League for a second season running. Its hoped‑for star of this decade, Rafael Leão, was ready to move on amid laments of unfulfilled potential.

Still, from day one, Amorim has given off the air of a cat who got the cream. It was tempting to infer some relief at moving on from an unhappy chapter at Manchester United. Certainly it can’t have hurt that Milan’s owners backed their new manager to a tune of more than €160m (£132m) on transfer fees in the summer window.

But there was something in there too, of a person fulfilling a promise they made to their younger self. “Everybody knows Milan is one of my clubs since I was a boy,” Amorim said. “In my time as a young boy, Milan was the strongest team in Italy. And calcio was the best league in the world.”

Serie A lost that title some time ago. No Italian team have won the Champions League since 2010, and no player representing one has been awarded the Ballon d’Or since 2007. The Premier League long ago surpassed all rival competitions for TV revenues and spending power. Only a handful of super clubs elsewhere have kept up.

And yet, Serie A is having some kind of moment. Its reputation as the home of dour catenaccio is as outdated as Amorim’s old VCR, but things have spun especially far in the opposite direction this season, with an average of 3.18 goals per game. Italy’s top division has become home to some of the giddiest attacking football on the continent. Through almost 10 completed rounds there have been two 0-0 draws.

Bologna 2-1 Monza, Udinese 2-5 Roma, Milan 3-1 Inter, Como 1-0 Venezia, Frosinone 2-0 Torino, Lazio 2-1 Cagliari, Lecce 1-2 Genoa, Juventus 2-0 Napoli

Monday: Sassuolo v Fiorentina (5.30pm GMT), Atalanta v Parma (7.45pm GMT)

Amorim’s Milan have played their part. On Wednesday they endured their first league defeat, a barmy 4-2 loss at home against Bologna in which they fell behind early, came back to lead before half‑time then collapsed after the interval. Their manager cited exhaustion. An ominous thought, leading into the derby on Saturday. Inter had dropped only two points all season. Even their one draw felt more like a win, coming from two goals down to get a result away at Roma. Reigning champions, who reinforced the deepest squad in Serie A with the English trio of Curtis Jones, John Stones and Djed Spence in the summer, the Nerazzurri have been strong favourites to retain their title.

But after waiting a lifetime for a part in this fixture, Amorim was never going to arrive unprepared. If anything, the defeat by Bologna might have been influenced by his keeping one eye on the derby. Luka Modric and Christian Pulisic were left out of the starting XI in midweek, coming on only as second-half substitutes. Both lined up at kick-off against Inter. So did several other starters who had been deemed unfit even for a place on the bench against Bologna – Mario Gila, Adrien Rabiot and Diego Moreira. Amorim sprung a surprise on top of that by naming the 20-year-old Sankhoun Diawara, whose only previous Milan start had been at centre-back, as his left wing-back in a 3-4-2-1.

The manager has shown more tactical flexibility at Milan than he did in Manchester, alternating his back three with a four. In the biggest game of his Milan tenure to date, however, Amorim returned to what he knows best. And Cristian Chivu copied him.

Inter’s manager was grappling with an availability crisis up front. Lautaro Martínez has been out for weeks with a hamstring strain, while Francesco Pio Esposito and Ange-Yoan Bonny were unfit to start due to a virus. Chivu adapted by pushing Andy Diouf, a former midfielder who has been thriving at wing-back, forward to play on the right shoulder of Marcus Thuram, with Petar Sucic on the left.

But where the Nerazzurri looked unsure of themselves in a new system, Milan were straight into their stride. Pulisic put them in front in the fourth minute, his thumping header from Moreira’s cross the culmination of 80 seconds of unbroken possession. Rabiot then made it 2-0 in the 10th minute with a magnificent first-time flick across his body at a corner.

Inter’s defending, on both occasions, was horrendous, but that can be acknowledged without diminishing Milan’s design. The Rabiot goal was a rehearsed training ground routine, Diawara crossing paths with the Frenchman and blocking Hakan Calhanoglu’s attempts to track. Moreira was also flawless in his deliveries. The derby became his breakout moment, showing why Milan spent more than €50m to sign him from Strasbourg this summer.

Inter have recovered from losing positions five times already in this Serie A season, and three times from 2-0 down. They were threatening to repeat the trick after Alessandro Bastoni pulled a goal back from a corner. Spence forced a sensational save from Mike Maignan. But Milan won a free-kick, 20 yards out on the right. Moreira asked Modric to let him take it, then whipped a left‑footed shot over the wall into the near side of the net.

The game finished 3-1 to Milan, Inter’s first league defeat and a huge lift for Amorim. Despite being unbeaten themselves before the midweek defeat by Bologna, the Rossoneri have not always convinced. Even when controlling the tempo of games, they seem to lack clarity in the final third. Gonçalo Ramos, the club’s record signing, has not looked a natural fit as a lone striker, dropping deep too often when his team need a presence inside the box. He has scored just twice in 10 starts since his €73m move from Paris Saint-Germain.

Even this win raised questions. Can it really be the long-term vision for Moreira, the right wing‑back, to frequently hold a position on the pitch higher than the centre-forward?

Amorim was quick to insist on Saturday that no one should get carried away. He expressed delight for supporters and described the experience of his first Milan derby as unlike any other game of which he had been a part. But he also said Milan had been only good, not great, and noted that the three points here were only the same number they would have got by beating Bologna.

A sensible line to take. Milan have dominated this fixture lately – winning the past four derbies across all competitions and staying unbeaten in the past eight. Yet they have not finished above their neighbours since 2021-22, their last Scudetto-winning campaign.

Still, beating your greatest rival is always better than the alternative. The club’s owner, Gerry Cardinale, has been vocal in backing the new manager, telling La Gazzetta dello Sport last week that he was all in on “Amorim ball”. But in the week that Milan and Inter jointly presented plans for the new stadium that will replace San Siro in 2031, this result added weight to his assertion that the Rossoneri can contend for a Scudetto too.

#965. How to become a football referee

Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and said sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your plan and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

With a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

If you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:

In her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees new referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she says. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared."

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she says. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

As well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful."

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.

Sources: National Careers Service, GOV.UK, FA, IFA, SFA, and FAW.

#963. 'My job combines my passion for gaming and football'

Working on one of the world's biggest football video games is the perfect combination of my two biggest passions, gaming and football.

I'm CJ Ramson. I work on the creation of football video games. I work on Football Manager as an associate QA manager. QA stands for quality assurance.

We're the ones that test the game. We make sure everything works, and we work closely with the developers to try and make the most realistic simulation of football.

Growing up, I loved football, whether that was playing football or playing football video games with my friends. I'd always be doing one or the other. With the video games, the thing that really drew me to them was I've always been into the tactical side of the game, either being able to control the players or create your own tactics.

So a typical day for us, we'll get a new build in from the developers. We'll test it as a QA team, and we'll look for either bugsor ways that we can improve the game. That can be anything from the runs that players make, to decisions they make on the ball, what the team instructions and tactics do. So there's a lot of areas for us to cover. Our final goal is to make it as realistic to real football as possible.

So even though my background was in coaching, there was a lot of transferable skills that I learned and developed through my time coaching that I managed to transfer into this. So whether that's being really analytical and having a good eye for detail and knowingwhen to pick things out and what to look for, or it could be things like timekeeping and making sure things run perfectly on time, and working with other people as well. So social skills where you have to work within a team or even lead a team.

The animation he makes, and the ball physics as well, where the ball goes off after the save."

So as much as I loved playing football, I realised quite early on I probably wasn't going to be a professionalfootballer. But I wanted to work in football and find. So at college, I studied sports science, and that's where I found my love of coaching. I did my FA Level 1 and then went on to do my FA Level 2. After I left college, I got a job at Arsenal, which was unpaid, working with them, learning how to develop my coaching skills. Which then led to me having a full-time paid job at Fulham Football Club, working with the youth teams, working with the academy teams. And then that eventually led to me going to an event. I saw an opportunity where you could apply for a job in Football Manager. It was something that naturally I was interested in, had a conversation with them, and realised it was definitely something that I would love to do.

So I went to the networking event at Kick It Out, and that was an opportunity for me to network with other football coaches, other people within the gaming industries, and have a really good insight to different jobs in football gaming. Without doing that, I wouldn't have the opportunity to meet the people at Football Manager and see a new job in gaming, which I wouldn't have beenaware of.

One of the highlights of my career so far is working on the in-and-out-of-possession system on FM 26. This is something we see in real football all the time, so being part of the team that brought that to life and brought it into the game was super cool.

Working within the football industry is a dream come true. Being able to work on something that I'm passionate about, that is played and enjoyed by millions of people, is an amazing feeling for me and an amazing opportunity that I have. And yeah, I love it.

To find out what other jobs you could have in football, explore the BBC Bitesize Follow Your Passion collection.

Ever wondered who makes sure your footy video games are great? This guy!

CJ works as an associate quality assurance manager on the video game Football Manager. His team test the game to make sure everything works, and collaborate with the developers to create the most realistic simulation of football.

There are lots of different ways to progress in the gaming industry.

CJ works in the QA (Quality Assurance) team, testing games. In this team, his career progression has followed this path:

His team is just one of the options, though. "There are lots of other roles within the industry too, including production, game design, social media and development, where developers help to code the game," he explains. "Depending on your skills and interests, there are different pathways you can take that you might enjoy and be suited to."

There are different roles in video game testing. CJ notes that: "Salaries can vary depending on your role and the company you work for. They can range from around Â£20,000 to Â£50,000 and upwards." The higher salaries in this range could apply when you've gained more experienced and progressed in your career.

CJ is now a quality assurance manager, but he started out as a quality assurance tester. Find out more about the role of QA tester below. This role can have various other job titles, such as games tester, computer games tester, and video games tester.

You could get into this role via a university course, a college course (such as a Level 3 Diploma in Creative Media, an A-level in Computing, or a T-level in Digital Software Development (England only)), an apprenticeship, or applying directly if you have relevant experience.

#962. Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or party gives way to anxiety-filled hangover for Bayern Munich | Andy Brassell

Dortmund did not read the script, remaining level on points with the defending champions at the top of the table

It was the moment they had all been … not so much waiting for, but planning, pushing and yearning for. In the videos that announce the starting lineup on the giant scoreboard before kick-off, every Bayern Munich player turns to face the camera with their personal salute, greeting or goal celebration, the playful progression from the standard folding of arms. Except on Saturday evening, the No 9 turned around smiling, and cradling the golden trophy.

In the midweek DFB Pokal stroll against Magdeburg there had been a salute, the players welcoming Harry Kane on to the pitch with a guard of honour to commemorate his Ballon d’Or victory two nights before. This, however, was the real party, the moment where the England captain’s and Bayern’s successful union and the apex it has reached was celebrated in front of a global audience. There was every reason to believe it would be a full and satisfying victory lap, even in Der Klassiker, with proper competition so often bringing the best out of the Rekordmeister.

Dortmund, however, did not read the script. Neither did the football gods. Kane was not completely neutered in this and laid on yet another assist, nodding across goal to present Dayot Upamecano a second goal in successive Bundesliga games That looked like the winner until Fábio Silva’s 89th-minute equaliser for the visitors. Yet in between, there was frustration for the man who has walked on water since arriving in Munich. He clattered a penalty which could have made it 2-0 against the crossbar and hit the post from point-blank range when he could have made it 3-1, after Serhou Guirassy’s first equaliser and the Upamecano strike that put Bayern back in front.

Three years ago on Wednesday, Kane hit a hat-trick in his first Klassiker in a 4-0 win at Signal Iduna Park. Despite the cliche that BVB are Bayern’s bunnies, the champions have not had it all their own way in this fixture. This was Kane’s fourth Klassiker at the Allianz Arena, and Bayern have only won one of them. Many of those watching from around the world who tuned in to see Kane lift his personal trophy would have expected a subsequent procession to victory but having arrived level on points at the top of the table, Dortmund were able to leave Bavaria in the same position.

This was, as Ruhr Nachrichten’s Kevin Pinnow put it, “much more than just a point” for Dortmund. It was not a signal they are Bayern’s equal but a sign they could roll with the punches, that they could show guts and enterprise and find solutions, from the switch to a back four that blind-sided their hosts to the energy and daring in midfield, exemplified by Jobe Bellingham’s best performance since he arrived last year. The young Englishman is a symbol of the good Niko Kovac has done since arriving at the club, a combination of patience and high demand. The coach insisted earlier this year that Bellingham, despite a lack of numerical reward, was progressing ahead of schedule and this, finally was the proof. He might even have put BVB in front in the first half, but had a goal ruled out as the offside Carney Chukwuemeka – who also excelled – inadvertently stumbled into Jonas Urbig in the Bayern goal. “He is someone for the big stake,” enthused the sporting director, Ole Book. “He showed that today.”

SV Elversberg 4-1 Mainz, Augsburg 1-2 Freiburg, Mönchengladbach 0-0 Paderborn, Schalke 0-2 RB Leipzig, Werder 2-0 Hoffenheim, Leverkusen 2-4 VfB Stuttgart, Bayern 2-2 Dortmund, Union Berlin 1-1 Köln, Eintracht Frankfurt 3-1 Hamburg

Yet as worthy as Dortmund were, little went for Bayern. The bad luck was not limited to plural pinging of aluminium and the effects will last for longer than Monday morning. Already without Vincent Kompany, who will not be rushed back into action after his recent hospitalisation with his assistant, Aaron Danks, holding the fort, the injury list is getting out of hand. Danks went into this fixture without Luis Díaz, Manuel Neuer and Jamal Musiala and lost a further three forward players during the course of the evening.

Ismael Saibari injured his ankle ligaments in a collision with Gregor Kobel and has already had surgery, with the recovery to last at least three months. Serge Gnabry is expected to miss several weeks with a hamstring injury he picked up and, worst of all, Michael Olise went down off the ball with what appeared to be a knee problem in the closing minutes. Bayern will go into this week’s Champions League game with Atlético Madrid – surely the last game they would wish to face with a banged-up squad – with only two senior forward players available, Kane and the 18-year-old Lennart Karl.

Karl still almost won the game for the hosts, bending a shot from range against the top of the crossbar in stoppage time He might have many other chances to make himself the hero in the games to come. As will Kane, again and again. We will see quite how the immediate post-Ballon d’Or period will unfold. One of Kane’s key characteristics throughout his career has been his relentless availability, but part of his ascension to his best-ever self has been based on Kompany’s ability to rest his star turn and keep him fresh. With the current plethora of injuries, Danks is unlikely to have the same luxury.

It is impossible to talk about turning points in the season on Halloween. Yet Kane will be loading Bayern on his broad shoulders ever more than before, and Dortmund’s next challenge is to be brave enough to try to take advantage.

If Sebastian Hoeness and his Stuttgart team were going to lift themselves out of a crisis of confidence it was always going to be not by eking out a gritty result, but by blasting their way back to health, and that is what they did at Leverkusen, winning 4-2 in a fixture that has been one of the Bundesliga’s must-watch match-ups of recent seasons. For all their attacking punch, Hoeness and company arrived having lost four out of five on the back of some profligate finishing. Here they were clinical in a testy game against a Werkself team who had chances of their own. “Unfortunately, we can’t play Leverkusen 34 times,” lamented the Champions League joint top scorer Ermedin Demirovic, who scored twice. “They’re always heated and exciting matches because both teams play with attacking intent.”

Leipzig strolled to a 2-0 win at an impotent Schalke – still yet to score a home goal – before facing Manchester City, an important step to Martín Demichelis shoring up his position. The Norwegian winger Antonio Nusa, who scored one and made one, excelled.

Niclas Füllkrug was at it again for Werder Bremen, after an attempted midweek DFB Pokal rescue act at his old club Borussia Dortmund, scoring twice to bring Werder level before their hopes were dashed by a late Marcel Sabitzer winner. The centre-forward blasted the northerners into the lead on Saturday against Hoffenheim, setting up a win that pushes them into the top five. It was his seventh straight Bundesliga game scoring, equalling the legendary Rudi Völler’s record from 1982-83. “I’m truly speechless,” said the goalkeeper Karl Hein, whose huge clearance set the goal up. “It’s a privilege to have him with us.” Even with his plan to revitalise Germany and make the squad younger, it is hard to see how Jürgen Klopp can omit Füllkrug when he announces his next Germany squad on Thursday.

#959. Choke of the century? Chengdu collapse sets up thrilling Chinese Super League climax

John Aloisi’s players need a point on the final day to seal their maiden title – but their form has dropped off a cliff

With four games of the Chinese Super League to go, Chengdu Rongcheng needed just a point to clinch their first title. With one game to go, they still need a point. What was a formality has become a formidable task. The biggest bottle job in Asian football history is very much on and it would be as popular as it would be dramatic.

The coach of the Sichuan club, the former Portsmouth and Coventry striker John Aloisi, has seen a 12-point lead over Dalian Yingbo cut to just three before Sunday’s showdowns. Whatever happens, this is a positive and thrilling end to a season that started negatively – literally – with nine of the 16 top-tier clubs kicking off on minus points.

They had been punished as part of a “special campaign to crack down on match-fixing, gambling and corruption in the football industry”, said a joint statement from the Chinese Football Association, the Ministry of Public Security and the General Administration of Sport at the time.

Chengdu were one of the seven to start on zero, above the defending champions Shanghai Port, who lost five points, and the runners-up Shanghai Shenhua who were hit with 10. It robbed the usual favourites of energy and it was all a bit surreal.

It almost felt over as soon as it started with Chengdu opening up a big lead, dropping just two points from the first 12 games while the usual powers struggled to get going.

Chengdu is a major city known more for its fiery Sichuan cuisine, genteel temples and cute pandas than football, despite English attempts to change that. In 2006, Sheffield United bought a local club but the Chengdu Blades were eventually dissolved in 2015. Four years later, City Football Group bought a stake in Sichuan Jiuniu but then moved the club to the southern city of Shenzhen in 2024.

Chengdu Rongcheng were formed in 2018, coming up through the divisions to finally, this season, be within touching distance of the championship. But just two wins from the past 13 and three defeats in a row mean the leaders are not limping to the line but have collapsed right next to it.

It should have been over weeks ago. On 10 October, more than 40,000 fans were ready to celebrate the title but an added‑time goal from Alberto Quiles gave Tianjin Jinmen Tiger a 1-0 win and postponed the celebrations. Next up was a trip to Shanghai Port but that ended in a 3-0 defeat. The penultimate game of the season came against challengers Dalian Yingbo, when again, just avoiding defeat was needed. It was another painful experience as they lost 1-0 after missing a first-half penalty and having a 90th-minute equaliser ruled out by the video assistant referee.

Chengdu have not scored in almost seven hours of football while Dalian are the form team with four consecutive wins. If they win a fifth against Tianjin then Chengdu need a point at fourth‑placed Shandong Taishan as the league is decided by head-to-head results before goal difference. Not many think they will. Even fewer hope so. Dalian and the 60,000 fans who attend home games are the people’s choice. Chengdu are not popular because their fans have developed a poor reputation. Last November, the club were fined about $70,000 (£52,200) after some home supporters racially abused Henan FC’s Ghanaian striker Frank Acheampong, just weeks after a punishment of $3,000 after travelling supporters at a Champions League game in South Korea threw bottles at the Ulsan HD players.

Whatever happens it is an unexpected and dramatic ending to a season that started in shock and the usual negative international headlines that surround Chinese football. The grandstand finish is welcome and average attendances have risen. They are poised to finish at about 30,000, a considerable jump from 25,755 last season and, by some distance, the best in Asia. Regional leagues have been enjoying some popularity too, showing that there is genuine love for the game in the country; a passion that grows better when it is organic from the bottom rather than organised from the top.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The national side is still a problem, though, and even for a fanbase well accustomed to disappointment the recent 5-0 defeat against Palestine at home, the fourth-biggest loss in history, was tough to take. As one journalist said, being thrashed by Brazil, Japan and Wales is one thing, but Palestine was another. There were some mitigating circumstances in that a number of national team players were at the Asian Games, where China actually performed well, losing narrowly against South Korea in the bronze final.

There are signs that the gap behind Korea is not as wide as it used to be. China reached the final of the under-17 and under-23 Asian championships this year before losing both against Japan. Compared with the rest of Asia’s best, young Chinese players are closing the gap at a technical and tactical level. Exporting more players to Europe is necessary to play at a higher level and if that happens, that senior national shirt may feel a little lighter.

Failure can, however, be hard to shake off as Chengdu Rongcheng may well find out if they mess this up.

#958. Why are some football shin pads so small?

Liverpool striker Lewis Koumas (second from left) sported low socks and small shinpads on his full Premier League debut at Anfield

Liverpool's Lewis Koumas made his full Premier League debut against Manchester City on Sunday.

While doing so, he sported some very low socks over what appeared to be a very small shin pad.

Last season, images of Burnley's Marcus Edwards went viral after the 27-year-old was seen wearing barely visible shin pads during a Premier League match against West Ham.

Two years ago, a picture of teenager Harry Howell celebrating with James Milner while they were Brighton team-mates also gained attention after fans noticed the visible difference in the size of their shin pads.

Howell's 'micro' pair were an obvious contrast to Milner's far more traditional-sized guards.

So what is behind the trend of extra-small shin guards, and why are they used instead of regular-sized pairs?

The simple answer is that players can choose what size shin pads they want to wear.

The International Football Association Board (Ifab), responsible for the laws of the game, say that shin pads are a mandatory piece of equipment players must wear while playing.

Be of an appropriate size to provide reasonable protection and be covered by the socks

And players are responsible for the size and suitability of their shin pads

The law does not define what an "appropriate" shin pad size is, but leave that decision to each individual player.

Shin pads provide vital protection for players to prevent serious injuries.

There has been a rising trend in younger footballers, as well as some big stars, wearing small shin pads during matches.

The reason for this could be for more comfort and to allow players to move around with greater ease.

Referees are only required to check that some form of shin guards are being worn, Ifab told BBC Sport.

Ifab said players - or the parents or guardians of youth players - must take responsibility for their own safety on the pitch.

While shin pad size is ultimately an individuals choice, any decisions around player safety would also be made in consultation with their club and medical staff.

Marcus Edwards last year was seen wearing very small shin pads for Burnley in the Premier League

Grassroots football teams have started to ban small shin pads for safety reasons.

There are concerns that small shin pads do not cover the shins properly, which can lead to an increased risk of injury - especially at non-elite level.

In August 2024, a football club banned small shin pads after a youth player suffered a double leg break.

Penistone Church player Alfie Collins broke his tibia and fibula in a tackle during a game. The teenager's shin pads, which were no bigger than a credit card, were similar to a size recently worn by some stars of the professional game.

Shin pads "play an important role in injury prevention as they are intended to protect the shin from injury", the Football Association said.

"'Micro' or 'mini' shin pads may therefore increase the risk of injury due to the smaller amount of shin covered compared to larger sized shin pads," they added.

Diego Demme explains why he retired from football at 34 years of age

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For 16 years, football was Diego Demme's way of life. It took him from the lower leagues of German football to the heights of the Bundesliga and Serie A, where he helped RB Leipzig establish themselves among Europe's elite, and Napoli end a 33-year wait for the Scudetto.

But after suffering two serious head injuries in the space of four months, Demme faced a difficult choice: continue playing the sport he loved or risk jeopardising his health and his family's future. On September 23, the former Germany international announced his retirement from professional football.

"I retired because of the two head injuries I had in the last two years. That was a difficult time for me, and that’s why I decided to finish my career," Demme admitted to FourFourTwo. "I wanted to stop while I was healthy, and after the problems I had with my head injuries, I decided to not take any risk again on the field."

After developing at Arminia Bielefeld and Paderborn, Demme helped Leipzig achieve two promotions, reach the 2019 DFB-Pokal Final and become Champions League regulars, before swapping the Bundesliga leaders for a Napoli side in crisis.

Demme helped Napoli win their first trophy in six years with the 2019/20 Coppa Italia before winning the 2022/23 Scudetto. After four and a half years in Italy, he returned to Germany in 2024, initially taking on the captaincy at Hertha Berlin. However, his homecoming soon turned into a nightmare.

On September 15, 2024, Demme took a knee to the chin during Hertha's 2–0 defeat to Fortuna Düsseldorf. Although he initially continued playing, he subsequently experienced headaches, dizziness, and problems with his right eye.

Four months later, Demme was struck in the temple by a ball from close range during training, causing him to lose consciousness. The consequences lingered, with recurring headaches, dizziness, and psychological difficulties contributing to 27 missed matches across his final two seasons.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"It was a difficult situation. I felt very bad due to the concussions, and that was the first time I felt, ‘What the f**k is going on?' I couldn’t drive the car. I needed to be there for my kids, and I couldn’t. I have a wife and family, and the most important thing was to be there for them, so I felt it was better to stop football."

Despite attracting interest from Italian clubs including Empoli, Cesena, Catania and Sorrento, Demme decided against extending his playing career. Retirement, however, has hardly meant slowing down.

The 34-year-old is now running two Neapolitan pizzerias in Berlin, overseeing the construction of his house in Kleinmachnow and pursuing qualifications in padel coaching and sports massage. Above all, he is enjoying more time with his daughters, six-year-old Gia and three-year-old Ellie.

Nor has he abandoned competitive sport. Alongside training in boxing, grappling and mixed martial arts, Demme is returning to football with Plyrs United in the Icon League, the indoor small-sided competition founded by Toni Kroos and Elias Nerlich.

"I didn't want to join another club where I'd move due to the fact that my eldest daughter started school this summer, so I decided to stop. But now, I feel good again, and I feel like the old Diego before my injuries. I will play the Icon League because the physical risk isn't as much as a regular Bundesliga match."

From the Coppa Italia to the Scudetto, Demme has spent his career chasing football's greatest prizes. Now, he's found a reward that no trophy can match: the chance to grow old in good health and watch his daughters grow up.

Fluent in Spanish, Portuguese and Italian, Lowy’s versatile skillset has allowed him to traverse a number of different fields when covering major competitions like the FIFA Club World Cup. In addition to football, he is also a seasoned participant of other sports like pickleball, tennis, and volleyball.

#956. Azeez to Andrés: seven smart-looking Premier League deadline day deals

An 18-year-old who has played at two major international tournaments and the division’s top clearance maker from last season also feature

A tricky, exciting, quick and versatile midfielder, Azeez has proven himself in the Championship with Millwall over the past two seasons and now deserves a chance to test himself in the top flight.

Brighton had been chasing him for a while and struck a deal on deadline day for a very reasonable reported initial £12.5m, rising to £15m. If he can make the step up and produce anything like his second-tier form, he’ll be a steal.

He is a high-volume producer at the sharp end of the pitch, constantly making things happen that threaten the opposition’s goal, but standing out most for his crossing. He ranked top of the Championship last season for open-play crosses (227) and expected assists from crosses (6.71 xA).

He also ranked fourth for dribble attempts (131), ninth for shots (95), sixth for chances created from open play (58). He created good-quality chances, too; only two players created more big chances than he did (18), and he ranked fourth for expected assists. His 9.12 xA alongside only seven assists suggests he may benefit from playing alongside better finishers.

A hugely exciting prospect. Despite being 18, Mbaye has significant and noteworthy experience under his belt. Last year he made six appearances, including in the final, for Senegal at the Africa Cup of Nations and this summer he made four appearances at the World Cup. He has also played in two Ligue 1 title-winning campaigns, including 2024-25, when he became the youngest player in PSG’s history to start a game, and won the Champions League in both of those seasons

He is a dribbling and ball-carrying menace, who always looks as if he’s about to do something special. Among players to play at least 900 minutes in Ligue 1 last season, he was 11th for carries (moving at least five metres with the ball) per 90, with 20.0, and 12th for progressive carries (moving at least five metres upfield with the ball) per 90, with 10.3. Most of the players above him in both lists are defenders, who naturally have more space to move into.

He was third for take-on-ending carries, or running with the ball for at least five metres before attempting to beat an opponent with a dribble, with 2.9 per 90. And he also has end product to boot. He scored at Afcon and the World Cup despite limited minutes and his 0.45 goals or assists per 90 for PSG last season is not to be sniffed at.

Danso had a pretty impossible task over his two years at Tottenham. He was the back-up to the first-choice centre-backs Cristian Romero and Micky van de Ven, playing intermittently on both sides of central defence in dysfunctional teams jumping between styles of play, and he very rarely played for any consistent run of games.

He was unfairly compared with the players he was replacing for much of his time there, but the truth is he was always reliable enough. He excelled, however, when Romero got injured during the run-in last season and he was called upon in Spurs’ time of need as they scraped clear of relegation.

He may not be the best on the ball – though he is hardly terrible – but he is an excellent deep defender. Among those to play at least 1,000 minutes in the Premier League last season, Danso ranked first for clearances (8.2 per 90) and headed clearances (6.3), and was fifth for aerial duels won (4.8 per 90).

He could thrive at Sunderland, who spent more of their out-of-possession game time in a low block than any other team in the Premier League last season (25%). Danso could be perfectly at home in this setup, paired alongside the player he beat into second place for clearances and headed clearances: Dan Ballard.

It was always said during Pep Guardiola’s time at Manchester City that attackers had their wings clipped in terms of individual freedom, limited to playing within the parameters of the manager’s meticulous gameplan.

But dribbling ability became increasingly important in the final years of his reign, with Jérémy Doku and Antoine Semenyo on the wings and Rayan Cherki in between. Doku (162) and Semenyo (144) ranked first and second for dribbles attempted in the Premier League last season, with Cherki ninth (111). They also ranked first (84), fourth (59) and eighth (51), respectively, for dribbles completed.

With the deadline-day addition of Ndiaye, City have gone in even harder on dribbling ability under Enzo Maresca. The Senegal international ranked second for dribbles attempted (136) and dribbles completed (73) in the Premier League last season.

Fernandez-Pardo’s versatility is a major attraction. He’s comfortable playing off the left and cutting in on to his right foot, or as a No 9. Although not the bulkiest, he has explosive pace and promises to be a threat in behind.

The Belgium international is arguably at his most threatening when running with the ball because he does so with such purpose. His 122 carries progressing the ball at least 10 metres upfield in Ligue 1 last term were bettered by only seven players, several of whom were defenders.

On top of that, he ranked top for carries into the penalty area (69) and seventh for carries ending with a shot or chance created (39).

Fofana appeared to be enjoying a swift rise in 2024-25, only for a serious ankle injury to massively disrupt his development in 2025-26. Sunderland will be hoping they can get him back to the levels shown the season before last, when he was a real livewire on Lyon’s left flank.

He contributed nine goal involvements (five goals, four assists) in 1,586 minutes in Ligue 1 in 2024-25, averaging one every 176 minutes. Only eight forwards (900+ mins) averaged more expected assists per 90 (0.25).

The most eye-catching aspects of his game, however, were his dynamism and pace. He could be difficult to stop once moving, and this made him a very useful outlet. Among Ligue 1 forwards (900+ mins), his 16.6 carries per 90 ranked him sixth, and he moved up to third for progressive carries per 90 (11.5).

Fofana is direct, exciting and has significant potential. He is a player Sunderland could make a profit on if he reaches the levels previously expected.

Andrés arrived to bolster Brighton’s midfield options after Carlos Baleba’s exit to Manchester United. Although a different type of midfielder to the Cameroonian, Chema is another with vast potential.

A product of Real Madrid’s academy, Chema joined Stuttgart last summer. During his sole campaign in the Bundesliga, he was in and out of the team but caught the eye at the base of their midfield.

Comparisons have been made to Rodri because of his physical attributes and nominal role as a holding midfielder. He doesn’t have anything like the same influence in possession but Chema is tidy on the ball.

It’s what he offers defensively that is most notable, however. He’s been broadly praised for his anticipation and reading of the game, ranking second among midfielders (900+ mins) since the start of last season for interceptions per 90 in the Bundesliga (2.3).

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

David Warner has thrown his full support behind former Australia opener Usman Khawaja, who claimed that the side's entire dressing room knew about the ball-tampering scheme in Cape Town in 2018.

Khawaja has claimed in recent days that players and coaching staff were aware of the ball-tampering that occurred in South Africa eight years ago, stating: "It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us."

Warner also claimed the investigation held by Cricket Australia in the aftermath of the ball-tampering controversy was "rushed and botched".

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Warner and fellow batters ‌Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft were banned over the plan to rough up the ball with sandpaper ​during the third Test at Newlands in Cape Town.

In an excerpt of his autobiography released on Saturday, Khawaja said "open, lighthearted discussions" about tampering were ​not confined to batters, bowlers or staff but extended throughout the team.

On ‌Sunday, he added that he had chosen to speak about the 'Sandpapergate' scandal now after promising childhood friend Warner that ​he would share his side of the story.

Until now, nobody else involved in the tour has ever admitted culpability.

The bowling unit of Pat Cummins - now Australia captain - Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon even released a statement in 2021 denying they knew anything about the tactic.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Warner said in a video statement on Instagram: "People wanted to know it, you've come out and said it, and now people are saying, 'Why eight years on?' and talking about selling a book.

"This is Usman's story. This is what Usman believes. Uzzi wrote down every single thing from that day on. Uzzi, thank you.

"Now, this whole interview process was rushed and botched. Uzzi was sitting next to Cameron Bancroft. Uzzi was not interviewed. How is that a thorough investigation? It baffles me.

"We're not here to point fingers and we're not opening old wounds. It's about accountability, transparency and ensuring that the truth is properly examined."

Warner, who retired from cricket's traditional format in 2024 with 112 Test caps, said he decided to comment now after talking to his young daughters over recent days about what transpired in that match and later.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"Perhaps it's time people stop scrutinising the person asking for accountability and start asking those responsible for the investigation to provide it," he continued.

"Now, there have been a lot of statements and inaccuracies over the last eight years that were out in the media by people and there were a lot of people who stayed silent.

"The last couple of days I've been talking to my daughters and that's why it's taken me a couple of days to get this out, because I've had to tell them exactly what happened.

"Especially my 12-year-old Ivy, who wanted to know why we were holding her, why there were so many cameras and why we were crying on TV. That was a hard thing to do.

"But one thing I did say was, 'Girls, tell the truth, because lies will eventually come out'. It's a very tough time.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"This is for everyone in Australia. It's been the question that everyone's been asking. Uzzi, you said it how it is. It's 100 per cent accurate.

"It's been a tough time for my family, Steven and Cameron, no doubt, but this is what needed to come out. I fully support that, Uzzi."

Australian opener Nic Maddinson said it was "disappointing" that Warner, Bancroft and Smith had to "relive" the situation.

"It's obviously disappointing that it keeps coming up," Maddinson told 10 Sport.

"But it's that time of year, isn't it? Christmas comes along and people have books to sell.

"Things come out. It's just disappointing.

"I think the three guys who were affected the most, it doesn't really help them at all to relive it. Especially over the past month having [had a] great series in South Africa.

"Obviously, the crowds weren't as hostile maybe as people expected. But that stuff is still there every day at airports, with the general public making comments here and there.

"So, I guess over time [it] would still wear them down. It's just popped up again. Start of the summer, going into a pretty big six months for the team, it is obviously probably pretty disappointing for those guys."

#954. Were any current Man City players signed during charges period?

Manchester City captain Ruben Dias has made more than 250 club appearances since his arrival in 2020

No member of Manchester City's current squad was signed during the period in which an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

Those offences all came between 2009 and 2018. City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed against all of the charges against them.

The club's longest-serving first-team player who was purchased from another club is Portuguese centre-back and club captain Ruben Dias, who joined from Benfica in 2020.

Norway striker Erling Haaland is the next longest-serving arrival, joining from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2022.

Midfielder Phil Foden is the only player to have played for the club during the period in which they breached the league's financial rules, but was not a senior signing having come through the club's youth ranks.

Foden, 26, made his first-team debut in a Champions League match against Feyenoord in November 2017.

Like Foden, versatile midfielder Rico Lewis is also a product of the club's academy but did not make his senior debut until August 2022.

All of the club's other senior players were signed between 2023 and 2026.

#953. These AI agents design your perfect robot-powered lab — and run it for you

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Artificial-intelligence agents can devise a detailed procedure for a robotic arm and test it in a virtual laboratory.Credit: Jiaru Bai & Yuchi Zhao, University of Toronto

Laboratory robots are tireless and uncomplaining, but they have narrow skill sets, limited mobility and an inability to get out of each other’s way. Now, a system of artificial-intelligence agents promises to help lab robots do their best work.

In this process, a scientist describes their research programme and lab set-up to the agents, which then create step-by-step experimental protocols for the lab’s robots. The agents also generate a virtual version of the lab and test the protocols there. They can then direct the robots in the real lab to perform the research.

Robot chemist sparks row with claim it created new materials

Robot chemist sparks row with claim it created new materials

The agents can even design an entire lab from scratch, using a virtual one to work out the ideal placement for instruments and robots.

The system is described in a preprint posted in October to arXiv1. It has not been peer reviewed.

In a test, the agents wrote more than 200 commands directing a robotic arm to move between and interact with instruments in an existing lab space. The agent simulated the steps in the virtual lab to ensure that it all worked smoothly, then directed the real-life arm to carry out procedures to measure the optical properties of nanocrystals.

The concept is “very cool” and could drastically reduce the effort required to set up automated labs, says Evan Collins, a bioengineer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. But integrating the cameras and sensors that the agents need to direct experiments effectively could require more resources than does setting up a lab manually, he says.

The simulations would make it easy to plan robotic movements that avoid collisions between robots and other objects in the lab, says Collins.

This could ease the process of getting labs up and running, given that setting up an automated lab is often a time-consuming process of trial and error followed by extensive testing and troubleshooting. Because the agents conduct all the planning and testing in a simulated environment, there is no need for researchers to “babysit the system” after it’s built, says Yuchi (Allan) Zhao, a roboticist at the University of Toronto in Canada and co-author of the preprint.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03587-x

Bai, J. et al. Preprint at arXiv https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.23826 (2026).

#952. HENRY WINTER: Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton & Hove Albion are perfectly set up for success - on and off the pitch
