#839. What can you read into Premier League table after 10 games?

Only four teams have taken more points than Arsenal's 27 after 10 games

We are now more than a quarter of the way through the Premier League season, with each team having played 10 games.

History suggests the answer is quite a lot.

Last season, for instance, the top two - and two of the eventual bottom three - were in the exact spots at this stage that they in finished six months later.

How the Premier League table looks after 10 games

Arsenal are top of the table on 27 points - which is higher than the average number of points (23) champions have after 10 games.

In fact, only four teams have taken more points from their first 10 fixtures than the Gunners, and all four have gone on to win the league.

One small quirk that means Arenal fans should not start making plans for a parade just yet is that the only two previous sides to post exactly 27 points at this point of the campaign both failed to win the title - including the Gunners in 2022-23.

In 15 of the 34 Premier League seasons to date, the team top at this stage have gone on to win the title, so less than half the time.

While on 14 previous occasions, teams on 21 points, the tally of second-placed Brighton, or fewer after 10 games won the title, so there is still hope for the Seagulls.

However, the less good news for Fabian Hurzeler's side is that, bizarrely, the team in second after 10 games have won the title in just one of the past 18 seasons - that was Manchester City in 2022-23.

The fewest points any side has had at this stage and gone on to win the league is 18 - so City, on 21, and Liverpool, on 18, could still have a say.

Arsenal lead Brighton by five points, one fewer than the most points a team have ever come from behind at this stage to win a title.

Manchester United in 2002-03 and Manchester City in 2013-14 are the two to do that.

But Mikel Arteta and co can take comfort knowing the leaders at this stage have gone on to win the title in the past two seasons - after failing to do so in the previous four years.

Another 1-0 for relentless Arsenal - but did Odegaard spare VAR blushes?

Odegaard hits winner as Arsenal beat Hull to extend lead at top

Maresca's dream start turns into nightmare as title hopes hit

Crystal Palace are propping up the table having lost their past four league matches, but the stats suggest their position is far from terminal.

In total, 14 teams have stayed up having been bottom of the table at this point in the season - most recently Wolves in 2024-25.

Moreover, the fewest points a team has had after 10 games and stayed up at the end of the season is three.

That same Wolves team are the most recent of the four teams to have achieved that feat.

Sunderland, who climbed off the foot of the table with victory over Chelsea, had just four points at this stage in 2013-14 but still ended up finishing 14th.

Palace can also count themselves a little unfortunate to have amassed seven points and find themselves in 20th.

Only Bolton in 2002-03 have had more points (eight) after 10 games and been bottom - and that was in a situation when a number of other sides had played 11 matches.

Overall, 88 teams have previously had seven or fewer points after 10 Premier League games and 37 managed to stay up.

There is good news for Ipswich and Hull in that every promoted side since 2015-16 to take 11 points or more from their first 10 games - and there have been 14 of them - has survived.

The most recent promoted side to make as bright a start and go down were Cardiff in 2013-14, who were 12th with 12 points but finished bottom on 30 points.

The outlook is a little bleaker for Coventry.

Only two promoted sides in the past 11 seasons have taken fewer than 11 points and survived - Bournemouth in 2015-16 (eight) and Nottingham Forest in 2022-23 (five).

Frank Lampard's men are also the seventh promoted side to take exactly nine points from their first 10 games - two of the previous six survived (Wolves in 2009-10 and Leicester in 2014-15).

Lampard feels hair pull should have led to Coventry penalty

A long way to go then, still plenty of time for things to change. But how much do things really change from this point?

Well, not a great deal if we look at last season, when 15 of the 20 teams finished within three places of where they were after 10 games.

Aston Villa made the biggest jump, going from 11th at this stage to secure a top-four finish with time to spare.

So Champions League qualification remains well within grasp for Unai Emery's side, who are currently in 10th.

On the other extreme were Tottenham, riding high in sixth after 10 games before plummeting 11 places down the standings to finishing 17th, only securing survival on the final day.

As mentioned earlier, the top two and two of the eventual bottom three were already in their final positions by this point, while Burnley - the third relegated side - were only a place above the drop zone in 17th.

Perhaps Manchester United are in a relegation battle after all...?

#838. Who Is Justin Timberlake's "What Goes Around...Comes Around" About?

Justin Timberlake dispelled the longtime rumor that his 2006 hit “What Goes Around…Comes Around” is about his ex Britney Spears, revealing the real inspiration behind the track.

What goes around comes all the way back around 20 years later.

Nearly two decades after Justin Timberlake released his 2006 single “What Goes Around…Comes Around,” the Grammy winner set the record straight on the longtime speculation that the track was inspired by his breakup with Britney Spears.

“Maybe I should dispel a rumor at this point, which has gone around forever,” the 45-year-old shared on a Nov. 5 episode of Complex’s Re-Rank podcast. “It’s not a personal story from mine.”

In fact, Timberlake—who famously dated Spears from 1999 to 2002—said the song, which follows a woman who betrays her partner, before karma results in her facing the same fate,  is “actually a personal story from a friend” that he asked to use as inspiration for the track.

“He was just going through it, and he was telling me what had happened,” he recalled. “I said, ‘Do you mind if I write about this?’ And I quote, my friend said, ‘Yeah, torch that b--ch. What goes around comes around.’”

“And I was like, ‘I have to go. Thank you,’” Timberlake joked while pretending like he was on a phone. “He was like, ‘What?’ I was like, ‘I got it.’”

After ending the call with his friend, the “SexyBack” singer couldn’t stop the feeling of inspiration and immediately began writing.

“I hung up the phone,” Timberlake recalled. “I had the idea. I just went in and again, this song was written in, I mean, damn near 20 minutes. It was just flowing.”

He continued, “The interlude that goes with it, and then you put the video with it—there’s a 10-minute video we shot for it—this just hit on all cylinders for me.”

Because of this, the “Mirrors” artist noted that he would rank “What Goes Around…Comes Around”—the third single from his second album FutureSex/LoveSounds—as “one or two” if they were “ranking the bangers” from his discography. (He ultimately slotted it at No. 1.)

While Timberlake has now shared the way it was really going down when he wrote the hit, fans have long speculated that the Grammy-winning track was a sequel to his 2002 single “Cry Me a River,” which has also been believed to be about Spears.

After all, not only was the song released eight months after his split from Spears, but he also cast her lookalike in the music video.

And similar to “What Goes Around…Comes Around,” the lyrics quickly poured out of Timberlake.

“I wrote that song in about 10 minutes, five to 10 minutes,” he shared, confirming that he recorded “every vocal” within less than two hours.

For a look back at Timberlake’s journey in the spotlight, put on your suit and tie and keep reading…

#837. Crystal Palace poised to sack Pierre Sage and target Frank after Liverpool defeat

Frenchman under pressure after four successive defeats

Former Spurs manager Frank emerging as main candidate

Crystal Palace are poised to sack Pierre Sage after Sunday’s defeat by Liverpool left them bottom of the Premier League for the first time since December 2017, with Thomas Frank emerging as the main candidate to succeed him.

The Frenchman, appointed in mid-June to replace Oliver Glasner, has been under mounting pressure since a 5-0 defeat by Brighton last month. There have been few signs of improvement as Palace have slumped to four successive league defeats.

Sage has guided Palace to only two wins from their 10 Premier League games this season and they have the league’s worst defensive record, with 24 goals conceded so far. Although there were promising moments during the 3-1 defeat by Liverpool at Selhurst Park on Sunday, their habit of conceding goals from set pieces has not been rectified and it is understood the patience of the club’s hierarchy has worn thin despite Sage only being at the helm for 16 matches.

He is expected to become the first Premier League manager to be sacked this season on Monday. Palace are already believed to have started the process of bringing in his replacement. Frank, who was dismissed by Tottenham in February, spoke to Palace in the summer and is said to be keen for a new challenge after a successful spell at Brentford.

The former Nottingham Forest manager Sean Dyche also has his backers at Palace and would be seen as a safe pair of hands given his vast experience in the Premier League. Vítor Pereira, another former Forest manager, could be an alternative.

Sage signed a three-year contract in south London after leaving Lens, where he won the Coupe de France and qualified for the Champions League in his final season. Palace have lost their two main central defenders this year, Marc Guéhi moving to Manchester City in January and Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea in the summer. Two loan players – Axel Disasi and the teenager Honest Ahanor – were signed as replacements. Palace did not land one of Sage’s top targets, Malick Fofana.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Sage denied after the Liverpool game that his dream job had turned into a “nightmare” but suggested that Palace’s squad needed investment in January. “We have to adjust some positions during the winter transfer window to give more solutions,” he said.

"This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Voyager, 1, humanity's most distant spacecraft, is back in contact after briefly losing touch with Earth last month.

The spacecraft stopped phoning home for about 48 hours between Oct. 18 and 20 due to a communications glitch that Voyager 1 resolved on its own, before engineers could send the long-running spacecraft a remote fix.

"This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected," Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), said in an agency statement about the incident on Oct. 29.

Voyager 1 is almost one light-day from Earth, meaning that a command takes nearly a day to reach the spacecraft and a response takes another day to come back to our planet. The spacecraft will reach the light-day milestone on Nov. 18, at 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth.

NASA's Deep Space Network of three antennas does check-ins to make sure the spacecraft is doing well. On Oct. 18 and 19, Voyager 1 did not respond. Its signal fortunately reappeared on Oct. 20.

"Engineers still are investigating what caused the communication loss," JPL added in the statement, but said it appears Voyager 1 went into a sort of safe mode. "The team has so far determined that one group of thrusters went offline and their backups turned on. Such a swap is programmed to occur automatically if the spacecraft computers detect something amiss with the active thrusters."

Voyager 1 and its still-operational twin, Voyager 2, both launched in 1977 on an initial mission to explore planets in the solar system. The two spacecraft took advantage of a rare alignment that allowed them to swing from Jupiter to Saturn to Uranus and Neptune using a minimum of fuel, although funding to explore the more distant planets and moons was not guaranteed at launch.

The spacecraft duly swung by Jupiter's and Saturn's systems (some months apart from each other) to great acclaim before parting pathways. Voyager 1's close-up view of Saturn's rings as well as the moon Titan — which may have prebiotic or pre-life chemistry — altered the spacecraft's trajectory to put it high above the plane of the solar system. Meanwhile, Voyager 2 flew on to Uranus and Neptune in 1986 and 1989, respectively, providing the only up-close view of these planetary systems to date.

Running on nuclear power, and continuing to deliver valuable science from deep space, the Voyagers saw their missions extended repeatedly. Both crossed into interstellar space a few years ago, and are still operational.

But with age comes a cost: the plutonium power sources on both spacecraft are diminishing, requiring engineers to periodically shut off instruments or come up with other clever ways of saving power. Voyager 1 just underwent one of those power adjustments, nicknamed the "Big Bang" because it reconfigured a number of spacecraft instruments.

"In early September, engineers successfully turned off three devices on the Voyager 1 spacecraft and substituted them with three lower-power alternatives," JPL wrote of the effort, noting that Voyager 2 also had a "Big Bang" about six weeks previous to that.

JPL did not provide an estimate for how long the missions could keep running, but noted each spacecraft loses four watts of power a year — each launched with 470 watts — and that the spacecraft could continue operating science instruments "longer than previously anticipated" due to the Big Bang. On Voyager 1, for example, the falling power would have otherwise meant switching off another instrument possibly as soon as next summer.

In 2022, Suzanne Dodd, project manager for Voyager at JPL, stated the hope was the mission would continue to operate into the 2030s.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#834. Why Love Is Blind's Lauren Speed Thinks Her Engagement Ring Was Fake

Lauren Speed—who met and married husband Cameron Hamilton on season one of Love Is Blind—revealed what made her believe her engagement ring from production was fake: “I was heartbroken."

Lauren Speed is pods-tive that her initial engagement ring was a knockoff.

The Love Is Blind alum—who wed husband Cameron Hamilton during season one of the Netflix show—revealed why she thinks the engagement ring production provided for the couple was fake.

“I think they got real rings now, but mine was not,” Speed said on a recent episode of Cam Newton’s eponymous podcast. “The diamond fell out and turned green when I got in the pool.”

“I was heartbroken,” she added, “but now I think they have a jewelry partner, so they get real rings now.”

In addition to the couple’s engagement rings, Netflix also foots the bill for the brides’ wedding dresses, the wedding ceremonies and gives the contestants stipends for participating on the show, with Speed sharing that she and Hamilton received about $700 a week for their time filming the reality dating series.

And while the show’s participants can certainly clink their metallic wine glasses to that, the series’ creator Chris Coelen previously shed light on production’s bling budget, revealing that while all the couples' selected engagement rings have different prices, "it's generally in that $3,500 to $5,000 range...with some variations.”

And for anyone hoping for something a bit more extravagant?

"If they want to upgrade their rings, they're welcome to do that," Coelen continued to Entertainment Weekly in 2025. "We have nothing to do with that. We give them the rings, they do what they want."

Though it seems times have changed since Speed, 38, and Hamilton, 36, met and married while filming Love Is Blind in 2018, their bond continues to grow in the right direction.

In fact, the pair welcomed their first baby together, a boy named Ezra William Hamilton, last October following years of fertility struggles.

"To God be the GLORY!" Speed wrote on Instagram at the time, sharing that he arrived "a little earlier than planned, but perfectly on God’s time."

And while the path hasn’t been easy, the influencer would do it all again sight unseen for the life she lives today, noting how she was “healing, resting, and soaking up all the love."

Keep reading for more Love Is Blind secrets…

1. Are contestants paid to be on Love Is Blind? Former star Matthew Duliba said they are paid $5,000 to appear on the pod period of the show.

The real money is made in sponsorships afterward, as season two alums Deepti Vempati and Natalie Lee said they each made about $500,000 as influencers in under two years after their episodes aired in 2022.

2. Where do the cast members sleep while in the pods? According to Netflix, the contestants slept on cot beds in trailers next to the lounges during season one, but for season two they upgraded to hotel rooms to be more comfortable. They're escorted to and from their rooms by staff so they can't secretly see anyone.

"You're actually at a hotel," season four's Micah Lussier shared on TikTok in 2025. "That's where you're staying, and then the pods that you see is a set, so think of a big studio, and then the bathrooms are outside in trailers."

3. The reality stars don't get access to their phones starting in the pods until after they're back from their tropical vacation portion of filming.

Shayne Jansen shared of their vacations, "You don't have your phone or anything on you."

4. The pods portion of the experiment lasts about 10 days, with 40-50 hopeful singles serving as the initial cast. But over the course of the process, some singles are let go.

"There was a certain point where we did a whittling down of people just to focus internally on the people who were really connecting, to allow them more time," Love Is Blind creator Chris Coelen told E! News. "We ended up having maybe 20-25 people in the pods at that point."

5. The first dates between all of the singles were set up speed-dating style rotation, with everyone spending eight to 10 minutes with each person of the opposite sex. From then on, there were no limitations put on who you could talk to, when you could talk to them and for how long, as long as a production intermediary set it up as they were unable to communicate with each other outside of the pods.

6. According to Sal Perez from season two, the singles are given "talking points" and "questions" before heading into their dates, but they don't have to use them.

"There were kind of topics for the day," Kyle Abrams added in an interview with E! News. "It was good if there was a lull in conversation, you just refer to the little notebook and you can drum up conversation."

That being said, the show is far from scripted. As contestant Kelly Chase told Business Insider, "Although it might sound unbelievable (trust me, it was hard to believe myself), the show wasn't scripted for the cast."

7. As for what they eat on set? Kelly said that was one of the aspects of filming she enjoyed most, explaining that contestants are offered a wide range of options while in the pods.

"During the first 10 days of filming," she said, "we could choose from catered food that included options like grilled fish, chicken, steak, vegetables, pasta, rice, and fruit."

8. All the proposals happen on the same day, though some are shown earlier in the episodes to avoid watching them all back-to-back.

“Everyone gets engaged on that one day. And then the next day is the big reveal day," Kelly said, per Cosmo. "And then the couples separate and go back through their own door. You meet them [your partner] for 15 minutes—the person you just got engaged to—and then you don’t see them again for a few days. It’s crazy."

9. Where do the engagement rings come from?

"We supply them with the rings, and at that point, those rings are theirs," the creator told Entertainment Weekly in 2025. "They never have to give them back if things don't work out. They're their rings. And if they want to say that they paid for them, then that's up to them. They can say whatever they want."

10. Hosts Vanessa Lachey and Nick Lachey are no longer allowed to be at the reveals.

"We all used to be at the reveal," Vanessa told Parade in 2025. "So when they would come out on the red carpet, it was me, it was Nick, we had like the glam girls there, we had costume design, we had audio. We had everybody standing there."

But it ended up being "probably 50 people" in the room, which detracted from the romance.

"It got to a point where it got too loud," Vanessa added. "After that, they were like, 'No more people at the reveal. Just the cameras and the couple. This is their moment.'"

11. Hoping to see a few proposals, producers were not expecting more than five couples to get engaged in season one. So when two other couples (in addition to the six the show chose to follow) also ended the pod portion with an engagement, producers ultimately couldn't continue filming their journey.

"We felt like we wanted to tell diverse stories frankly," Coelen reasoned. "We weren't sure where the stories were going to go, everybody felt like they truly found the person they wanted to spend their life with and we had an abundance of story...we just didn't have time in the show to follow them, which is incredible to me."

12. One of those engaged couples was Rory Newbrough, who was often seen giving advice to the other men, and Danielle Drouin. They spent a week together in Miami as the other engaged couples went to Mexico to continue filming. But soon after they returned to Atlanta, they had a "very amicable" breakup when Danielle realized she still had feelings for another cast member, Matt Thomas. "She ended up wanting to pursue that," Rory explained to People. Danielle and Matt ultimately didn't last either.

13. The other unaired season one engagement was between Westley Baer, who was briefly shown discussing dating as a shorter man, and Lexie Skipper. Despite not continuing with the show, they dated for three months back in Atlanta. But Westley revealed to People that his career change caused their split. "I made a crazy decision to sell everything I owned, and I moved to Asia," he said.

Two season two couples—Caitlin McKee and Joey Miller and Kara Williams and Jason Beaumont—also got engaged, but didn't have their journeys filmed.

14. Are constants allowed to talk when there's not cameras around?

"In the pod stage, the answer is no," Micah said. "There's always cameras rolling in those pods. And when you're in the lounge, they don't want people talking if there's not cameras rolling, so it will be quiet on set. And that is because if you're talking about stuff, they can miss part of the storyline."

She said the experience in Mexico is similar.

"You won't fly together, you won't do anything off camera until they leave you alone in that room that first night," she said. "So, that's the first time that you get a talk off-camera."

But when they go home, there's more freedom to speak without being filmed.

"You have scheduled filming days, like every other day," she explained. "So of course, you get a ton of time off camera to get to know each other without them in your face."

"They pay for the dress," Micah said of the production team. "I remember when we went there were some dresses that were included and part of the budget, and we could choose from those. And there's a lot to choose from."

However, they also "had the option" to "upgrade" to a more expensive dress that they paid for. The season four star added, "To my knowledge, no one ever did that."

16. As for who paid for the weddings, a Netflix spokesperson revealed to Women's Health that production "supplies some of the basics, but because these are their real weddings, it's up to them as to how to spend their money." So the couples likely did have to cover some expense if they went over budget.

17. Despite some skepticism from viewers, the marriages are legit, with season one's Lauren Speed telling Refinery29, "This is a real legally binding marriage. This is not for TV. This is our life."

18. It's not random who goes first on the alter saying "I do" or "I don't," with Micah saying the production crew determines who goes first.

"It's not the officiant who decides," Micah revealed. "In my opinion, they will ask whoever they think is more likely to say 'yes' to go first, because then they get a two [person] answer."

Otherwise, she noted, "you don't have that chance of seeing the first person say 'yes' and having that shock."

19. So were the cast members obligated to make it to the altar? According to Coelen, they were not. "They certainly could choose to do whatever they wanted to do," he told E! News of the wedding day decision-making process. "Again, being there on the wedding day, I personally, knowing these people and their stories, I didn't know what was going to happen."

20. Then why do people wait until the altar to decide if they're going to say yes or no? While contestants aren't required to go through with the wedding day, there's a reason many do, even if they ultimately say no.

"In my experience, it wasn't like you have to get to the altar, like you must get to the altar," Micah shared on TikTok. "It was moreso being a part of the entire experience. The whole point of Love Is Blind is It's an experiment. And you wouldn't know if it's going to work or not unless you do the whole thing. So that was the thought process there."

21. Why do so few couples say “I do"? After only one pair of contestants tied the knot in season eight, Love Is Blind executive producer Ally Simpson provided insight into why it’s getting more rare for couples to make it past the altar, admitting that social media has made it challenging to recruit “nice men” for the experiment. She also noted that former contestant Chelsea Griffin joined the casting team to help mitigate the issue.

22. There were rumors online that Mark Cuevas, the youngest single man in the inaugural season, secretly had a girlfriend when he was on the show, which he later denied.

"I did not have a girlfriend the whole time," he said on the Be There in Five podcast. "I was single before [going on the show]. Now, being a single man, you're single, you're doing your thing. I'd never had a girlfriend before. Where was the time to be in a relationship during the experience?"

23. According to Kelly and Kenny Barnes, they never had any plans to actually get married at the end of filming season one. "We were adamant about we're not going to get married," Kenny told People. "And really, the engagement was just to extend the experiment. And we were both committed to that." And Kelly believed they were "going to continue dating, because that was communicated between us." That was until Kenny admitted on the wedding day he was not "emotionally available" to do so. "I felt very rejected," she admitted. "Like, 'That wasn't the plan. What the heck?'"

24. Jessica Batten, LIB season one's most polarizing cast member, claimed in an interview that she tried to quit the show but wasn't allowed to.

"I mean, I had to stay," she told EW. "I definitely had a conversation about leaving and I wasn't able to do that. My dog got sick too, and almost died during the show, I had so much other stuff going on."

She continued, "It was really frustrating because I kind of knew [Mark and I] weren't going to get there. I definitely had some conversations and attempted to leave, but I wasn't able to."

25. The season one weddings were actually filmed in the fall of 2018, meaning the two couples—Lauren and Cameron Hamilton, and Amber Pike and Matt Barnett—who actually decided to get married had to keep their relationships secret for 18 months before the show premiered.

26. Love Is Blind could go on and on for years, with Coelen telling E! News, "I'm thinking season 15" would be the last.

27. Did Carlton Morton look familiar? Well, it's because he's been on an ATL-set reality show before, popping up on The Real Housewives of Atlanta when he was working as Cynthia Bailey's assistant back in 2014. Bravo fans will remember he got into a heated argument with Kenya Moore, who had just joined the series.

28. Why does the show always have those gold cups? While fans have speculated the opaque cups help hide the amount of liquid in the glass to help with editing errors and cuts, Coelen said the goblets were chosen for aesthetics.

"When you turn on the show, you know it's our show," he told Variety. "It's a very authentic, really true following of these people's journeys, but I like the fact that we have this sort of connective tissue with that in a really light way, it's fun."

Deepti added to E! News, "We would always put all of our drinks in the gold goblets. It's just a symbolic thing for us."

Man Utd score twice in stoppage-time to share points in eight-goal thriller

After yet another breathless, chaotic, shambolic Old Trafford classic, Manchester United do not know whether to laugh or cry.

Their fans didn't, booing at some points, cheering at others.

Defender Diogo Dalot was singled out for gruesome treatment amid the second-half protests and songs of defiance as he was replaced by Patrick Dorgu in the 66th minute.

The players didn't, running away joyously to celebrate Dorgu's 96th-minute equaliser that made it 4-4 against Aston Villa.

They then applauded the supporters who stayed on despite the apparent hopelessness of the situation as the game entered injury time with United trailing 4-2, presumably to vent their anger on a day when defeat seemed certain.

Manager Michael Carrick was in spiky mood when he was quizzed about his future by Sky Sports reporter Patrick Davison.

"That's not going to happen," he said, when asked if he was going to walk away.

"Will there?" Carrick then added, when it was suggested there would "clearly be conversations" with United's hierarchy.

"You're telling me what you think," he responded.

"I'm quite clear what direction the club needs to go in. It's got to win games."

Sunday's ridiculous eight-goal thriller with Villa - a game in which the hosts twice fought back from two goals down - left United in the drop zone in 18th place. Their lowest position for 40 years after playing at least 10 matches.

As they enter the international break, they will spend more time in the relegation zone than they have done since 1986.

United have not won a league game since they beat Ipswich on 30 August, have conceded 15 goals in their past five games and conceded inside two minutes in three of their past seven matches.

Three minutes and 40 seconds was the earliest they have ever trailed 2-0 in a Premier League game.

Up next is a trip to Anfield to play rivals Liverpool on 22 November.

On the positive side, United's players have not downed tools for their manager.

Somehow, despite being two goals down on three occasions in the past two games, they have emerged with a win and a draw.

Added to a creditable first-half display in a 2-0 loss at Chelsea on 31 October where they had Lisandro Martinez sent off, before which Carrick was backed to turn the current situation round, was that enough for Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer family - and detached from this latest crazy day?

Was it enough for chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox who were at Old Trafford?

Four 'huge mistakes' that show Man Utd's defensive problems

Man Utd share 4-4 thriller with Villa but stay in drop zone

Dorgu makes dramatic impact - Man Utd v Aston Villa ratings

Carrick still in limbo & are Brighton title challengers?

Michael Carrick post-match interview - Manchester United v Aston Villa

"On the one hand it's dreadful to give up four goals at home," former United skipper Roy Keane told Sky Sports. "But they kept going, so you have to give them a little bit of praise.

"In terms of the bigger picture it's that rollercoaster of watching Manchester United. When you turn up most weeks there really is the feeling of not knowing what you're going to get."

Former United striker Dion Dublin offered his own take to BBC Sport, saying: "There's only so many times you can do that because it's quite tiring, physically and mentally. The players today were walking around after the game like they had lost, even though they got a point."

Some of the post-match interviews by United players backed up that observation.

"I don't feel happy - we are in a bad situation," admitted Dorgu. "We need to fight together to get out of it.

"Everyone needs to look at themselves and ask if they are doing enough. We need to fight for the manager, for the club and get out of this together."

The situation has not been made easier by fan sentiment.

Lack of form on the pitch, combined with the rising cost of ticket prices and a negative perception of how fans are being treated, has led to a negative reaction that is unprecedented in its ferocity since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.

A banner was hung from the second tier of the Stretford End shortly before the teams came out to start the game. It read "We don't want a new stadium, we want new owners".

Full-back Dalot was jeered off the pitch when he was replaced by Dorgu, the catcalls replacing the cheers that greeted his number being shown.

Joshua Zirkzee, who scored United's third in the second minute of injury time, suffered similar treatment during a game against Newcastle almost two years ago. The Netherlands forward was still on the bench when Dalot arrived and offered his team-mate a consoling hug.

Aston Villa boss Unai Emery was livid by his side's late capitulation, which cost him a first victory at Old Trafford.

Touted as a potential successor to Carrick, he regathered his composure after storming down the tunnel before the final whistle to assure United fans the club's results will improve.

"They have the capacity, power, players and everything to overcome this situation," said the Spaniard.

That is probably true. But from so many angles, the current position remains grim.

The Villa game was like a number so far this season - Everton away, Atletico Madrid away, Tottenham at home, Leeds away, Chelsea away - where either United have played well, or got themselves into winning positions in stoppage time and failed to secure victory.

Although the present situation can still be rectified, it now needs two lots of results to go Carrick's way for the table to look more positive. Yet how long will it be before it is accepted that such anticipated improvement is not going to materialise?

Can United afford to wait until the January window opens? Have they got the resources to spend in it when it does?

These are bound to feed into the thinking of Ratcliffe, the Glazers, Berrada and Wilcox as they consider the future - plus the attractiveness of potential replacements.

For now, Carrick is still looking to a future he is certain will be brighter than what he has just endured.

"There's more than enough," he said, when asked if he had seen enough to believe the current situation can be improved.

"Goals change games and you've got to deal with it. It's something we have to improve on drastically. We're just making it too difficult for ourselves at certain times.

"[The players] are switched on and concentrated, it's a variety of things. There's not a theme to it, apart from these one-off moments are catching us out at the moment."

#831. You don't have to go to the moon to see Earth differently: Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover on what really matters

After a record-breaking journey around the moon, Artemis 2 astronaut Victor Glover explains why you don't need to travel into space to see Earth differently.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Imagine traveling over 250 million miles from home, watching Earth disappear behind the moon and losing contact with the billions of people who call it home. What would you miss most? For Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover, the answer wasn't a particular place, a familiar view or even the comforts of home. It was something much more fundamental: human connection.

Speaking during a discussion with former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival on Oct. 18 in Tenerife, Canary Islands, Glover reflected on the extraordinary experience of traveling around the moon and how being so far from Earth had given him a renewed appreciation for the people living on it.

"The greatest reason to go to space, it isn't to be a swashbuckler hero," Glover said. "It's to do something that only 651 people have been able to do: miss Earth and miss other Earthlings."

Glover was one of the four astronauts aboard NASA's Artemis II mission, which launched on April 1, 2026, marking humanity's first crewed journey to the moon since Apollo 17 in 1972. Alongside NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, the crew traveled farther from Earth than any humans before them.

As the Orion spacecraft traversed the far side of the moon, the Artemis II crew watched Earth disappear below the lunar horizon before losing radio contact with our planet. Around 40 minutes later, Earth came back into view as the spacecraft emerged from behind the moon.

For Glover, however, the experience was about much more than the view. He believes that if everyone on Earth had the opportunity to make the same journey, they would come away with a similar appreciation for what they'd left behind.

"I think all of us would say something in our native language, in the most basic way we can communicate about love, joy, hope and inspiration," Glover said.

Although Glover shared the extraordinary journey with three fellow astronauts, the four of them were separated from the rest of humanity by hundreds of thousands of miles.

And for Glover, that distance brought with it a strange contradiction: the farther he traveled from humanity, the more he longed to connect with it."At the point of ultimate disconnection, [there is] this longing for connection," Glover said.

The experience gave him a perspective that he carried back into everyday life.

"There are moments where I am rushing through traffic and want to get where I'm going because I'm being selfish," Glover admitted. "But I don't have to stay there."

Instead, he remembers what it felt like to look back at a planet so distant that everyone who has ever lived could be covered by his hand.

"I wish you could all feel what it's like to come back home after that disconnection," he said.

Astronauts often describe experiencing the "overview effect", a profound shift in perspective that can come from seeing Earth from space. But Glover believes that there's something equally powerful waiting to be discovered much closer to home.

When asked by a Starmus VIII attendee whether people needed to undergo something extraordinary to develop a greater sense of kindness toward others, his answer was no.

Glover encouraged people to look more closely at the natural world around them, whether that meant walking along the beach, watching the ocean or simply examining a leaf held up to sunlight. Even something as ordinary as a leaf, he explained, is capable of turning sunlight into food through photosynthesis. And although science can explain how that happens, understanding the process doesn't make it any less remarkable.

"We have to choose to be moved by these things," Glover said.

He worries that modern life, with its endless technological distractions, has made it all too easy to overlook the extraordinary things happening around us.

"Familiarity breeds contempt. Have you heard this? I think it's worse than that. Familiarity breeds indifference," he said.

Glover has a name for this perspective he hopes people can rediscover without traveling into space: The sea level effect.

It's about finding the same sense of wonder and connection that astronauts experience in orbit, but right here on Earth, where most of us spend our lives. And ultimately, Glover believes the greatest wonder isn't the moon, the stars, or even the incredible complexity of nature. It's the people we share our planet with.

"I think the hardest place to see this miracle is in the actual greatest miracle in the universe: other humans," he said.

"We all feel it with babies, but when we get old enough to have opinions, we start to want to argue with each other."

Glover hopes that by taking the time to appreciate the natural world, people might become a little more willing to appreciate one another too.

"That's the mission that I want to be part of for the rest of my life," Glover said.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

#830. Medicinal plants, lessons from mushrooms and the power of smell: Books in brief

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Andrew Robinson is a writer based in London and author of Earthshock (1993), The Story of Measurement (2007) and Einstein in Oxford (2024).

Margaret Willes Bodleian Library Publishing (2026)

According to ancient Greek medical authority Hippocrates, “Nature itself is the best physician” — hence the title of writer Margaret Willes’s appealing book. Introduced with a substantial essay on European herbalism from medieval times to the present, it discusses 100 plants with medical properties, from alecost (Tanacetum balsamita, a member of the daisy family) to the yew tree (Taxus baccata). Each is illustrated with an exquisite colour drawing taken from John Gerard’s 1597 The Herball, or Generall Historie of Plantes.

When motor cars were invented in the late nineteenth century, their emissions were welcome at first, because they replaced the odour of horse dung that had reduced many city streets to “a state of organic olfactory crisis”, notes historian William Tullett. His engrossing history of smell ranges from ancient Christian aromas, through medieval Indian perfume and the scents of eighteenth-century slavery to the status of odour in twentieth-century China. It features “the foul, the fragrant, and everything in between”.

Jim Al-Khalili Princeton Univ. Press (2026)

Just before his death, Albert Einstein stated: “the distinction between past, present and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion”. In this compelling, if intellectually demanding, book about the physics of time, physicist and broadcaster Jim Al-Khalili disagrees. He argues that “the irreversible passage of time needs to be incorporated into the laws of physics”. By comparing the concepts of time in quantum mechanics, the general theory of relativity and thermodynamics, he concludes that time’s arrow is real, and makes the Universe tick.

#829. Kettering Town 'cannot hide' from racism problem

Kettering Town's director of football said the club could no longer hide behind "the comforting lie" that the abuse came from "a small minority"

Non-league Kettering Town have said they "can no longer hide" from the issue of racism after a visiting player was allegedly subjected to "sickening" abuse.

Redditch United player Dan Sweeney said he was targeted by a Kettering supporter during Saturday's Southern League Premier Division Central tie at the Poppies' Latimer Park stadium, which the hosts won 2-1.

The incident comes after a match official reported alleged racial abuse at a Kettering fixture last season, and a previous instance of alleged racist abuse against a Redditch player at Latimer Park in 2017.

In a statement, Kettering director of football Fabian Forde said the "poison" of racism went beyond matchdays.

He also spoke out against the presence of what he called "festering" racism on the club's fans forums.

Writing on the club's website, external, Forde said: "Let's be completely honest with ourselves: this is not the first time. We can no longer hide behind the comforting lie that 'it's just a small minority' or 'they don't reflect the majority of our fans'.

"Every single time we dismiss hate by calling it a minority issue, we minimise the damage. The truth is, if the majority stays silent, that small minority becomes our identity.

"They tarnish our reputation in the eyes of opposition players, fans, and officials. They make our club look like a haven for bigotry. Is that really who we want to be?"

Forde added that the club could not "keep sending out generic statements that mean nothing" and urged fans to support "real cultural change" by taking responsibility for calling out the perpetrators of racist abuse.

He said: "To the majority of our fans, the good, decent people who love this club for the right reasons, we are pleading with you.

"We need you to stand up. We need you to confront this minority head-on. If you see someone typing hate online, call them out. If you hear someone shouting abuse next to you on a Saturday afternoon, don't look away.

"Tell a steward. Identify them to the club. Why are we protecting people who are actively destroying the reputation of the club we love?"

Northamptonshire Police said Saturday's alleged incident had not yet been reported to officers

Northamptonshire Police said they had "not identified any report relating to this [Saturday's] allegation."

However, the force added: "It may be that any report is awaiting allocation or has been made to another police force. Should a report be made elsewhere and the alleged offence be found to have taken place within Northamptonshire, we would take ownership of the investigation.

"We note Kettering Town FC's statement that it is working with its security team, stewards and the relevant authorities to identify those responsible, and we would encourage anyone who believes they have been the victim of a crime to report it to police.

"Racial abuse has no place in football or wider society, and any reports made to us will be assessed and investigated appropriately."

In a statement, external, Redditch United chairman David Faulkner said: "I particularly welcome Kettering Town's commitment to working with its security team, stewards and the relevant authorities to identify those responsible.

"It is vital that this matter is taken seriously and that appropriate action follows.

"Tackling racism requires more than statements. It requires leadership, accountability and a collective willingness to challenge unacceptable behaviour whenever and wherever it occurs.

"We must never allow incidents like this to become normalised, dismissed or simply forgotten once the immediate attention has passed."

The Football Association has also been approached for comment.

#828. Lens were humiliated by Como. The pain continued against Marseille

Pierre Sage led Lens to second and glory in the Coupe de France last season. A lot has changed in the last six months

The Lens striker, Florian Sotoca, was completely motionless as he looked into the middle space from the bench. The game, finely poised at 2-1 with a few minutes remaining, was not beyond his side, but that is not the story his troubled face told.

Marseille had just restored their lead thanks to a goal from substitute Keyliane Abdallah. Bruno Génésio’s men would go on to take all three points and continue their unlikely charge up the table, but the atmosphere at the Stade Bollaert-Delelis was morose before Marseille had even stepped on the pitch. The match did little to lift the mood at the end of a week in which Lens made unwanted history.

A pre-match banner unfurled by Lens fans that called the players a “disgrace” had not even been put away when a miscommunication between Jonathan Gradit and Samson Baidoo gifted Marseille the lead after 82 seconds. The former’s pass dribbled towards the goalline and was tapped in by Amine Gouiri from just a yard out.

It was a disastrous start for Lens, who recorded the joint-heaviest defeat in Champions League history last week. The 9-1 thrashing by Como was also the heaviest home loss in the competition’s history. Yannick Cahuzac, the Lens manager, called it a “humiliation”. The club’s president, Joseph Oughourlian, scrawled the words: “never again” inside the dressing room. Losing to Marseille on Sunday was not as chastening but the defeat posed more questions about the club’s recent decisions.

When Cahuzac, a friend of sporting director Jean-Louis Leca, stepped up from his assistant role in September to replace Dino Toppmöller, who lasted just six games, there were accusations of cronyism. Cahuzac’s stint so far has been a poor advert for the practice.

After three defeats in the league, winless in the Champions League, a derby defeat to Lille, a record-breaking loss to Como, and the wheels have well and truly come off at Lens; the jury is out on whether Cahuzac can set them back in motion. It was one of his former teammates, Florian Thauvin, who equalised for Lens against Marseille – his former club – with a close-range header. The playmaker, a harsh omission from Zinedine Zidane’s latest France squad, has been a rare bright spot in an increasingly gloomy situation.

Génésio said earlier in the season that these were the kinds of games Marseille could compete in but not win. But, as the French maxim goes, “le foot va vite” (football moves quickly). The tide has turned in Marseille; five league wins in a row have taken Marseille from the relegation zone to the Champions League places.

Génésio says his team’s fragile revival exists on “a knife’s edge”, however recent results – including a win at Bayer Leverkusen in the Europa League last week – have fed into growing optimism that his limited squad (both in quality and quantity) might avoid the abject season that fans had assumed was inevitable. The achievement belongs to Génésio, as does this win, secured by substitute Abdallah.

The academy product was banished to the reserves after his performance against Le Havre last month. Génésio criticised “a kind of lobbying around the young players” (from whom he did not specify) and held firm on his stance. He got the desired response. Re-integrated, Abdallah popped up at the back post to give Marseille a win that has taken them up to fourth in the table. They were second from bottom before the last international break.

Lens have replaced Marseille as France’s crisis club. After the match the home players did a tour of the pitch, applauding the fans for their support. In response, the fans unfurled a banner that read: “Shame on you.” Le foot va vite. Just six months ago fans packed into the Bollaert in the wee hours of the morning to welcome home their heroes after they had won the Coupe de France final. That feels like a lifetime ago for the players, fans and Pierre Sage, the manager who delivered that trophy.

“We are sick,” admitted Cahuzac after the match. There has been soul-searching but also plenty of finger pointing. Cahuzac says he “isn’t worried” about his job. Despite the growing pressure, he certainly has reasons to feel reassured but his friend, Léca, is also under a bit of fire after a second summer transfer window considerably less successful than his first. Jean-Clair Todibo, Thorgan Hazard and Franjo Ivanovic all arrived with high expectations but have fallen way short of them.

The fans had a banner for Léca, too, calling out his “shit interview” after the defeat to Como. They wanted an “apology”. They did not get one but it is certainly a sorry state of affairs at Lens.

Monaco won their third game in a row in the Conference League last week, but their 1-1 draw at Le Mans was their fifth straight game without a win in Ligue 1. Filipe Luís says they need to “cleanse the minds” over the international break. When Monaco last won in Ligue 1 – against Lens in September – they were top of the table. They now sit seventh. The goals have dried up for Paris Brunner, Folarin Balogun – returning from injury – has yet to replicate the form that attracted Premier League interest and Matthis Abline put in an anonymous display against Le Mans. Monaco were reliant on a defensive blunder to open the scoring through Mamadou Coulibaly, who could be in trouble for a throat-slit celebration. Brunner was punished for a similar celebration earlier this season, although on that occasion it was directed towards the opposition fans. Le Mans, who equalised in the 90th minute through Erwan Colas, are also without a league win since September, but there was a strong show of support for manager Patrick Videira from the home fans, who also took a dig at the club’s unpopular football adviser Bruno Cheyrou. He evidently would not have popular support if he were to instigate a managerial change.

From cleansing minds at Monaco to exorcising demons at Nice. The club endured a shocking 2025-26 campaign, during which the relationship between fans, the players, and the club reached breaking point. It ended with Nice narrowly avoiding relegation to Ligue 2, thanks to a playoff win over Saint-Étienne. A new manager, Olivier Pantaloni, and a new sporting director, Roger Ricort, came in over the summer, but the players and Pantaloni continued to speak of the scars of the previous campaign. They showed in the opening four games, none of which Le Gym managed to win. Since then, however, only PSG have taken more points. Nice’s 2-0 win at Angers means they have picked up 15 points from their last possible 18. The club are now in European contention. Pantaloni is once again working his magic, just as he did at Lorient last season.

#827. Taylor Swift, Karlie Kloss Prove There's No Bad Blood at Chiefs Game

Taylor Swift and Karlie Kloss put feud rumors to rest as they cheered on the Kansas City Chiefs Nov. 8, just months after the supermodel attended the Grammy winner’s wedding to Travis Kelce.

If Taylor Swift and Karlie Kloss had problems, it looks like they were able to solve ‘em.

Four months after the model surprised fans with her attendance at the Grammy winner’s wedding to Travis Kelce, Swift and Kloss confirmed their friendship is far from ruined when they reunited at the Kansas City Chiefs game against the New York Jets at Arrowhead Stadium on Nov. 8.

To cheer on her guy on the Chiefs, Swift—who donned a striped red sweater—was joined in her suite by Kloss as well as her and Joshua Kushner's 5-year-old son Levi. Also stopping everything now to support Kelce were the "Opalite" singer’s parents Andrea Swift and Scott Swift, plus her mother-in-law Donna Kelce.

Swift, 36, and Kloss, 33, were all smiles as they supported the “Love Story” artist’s husband during his milestone 200th game in the NFL, with the pair even standing up to applaud and share a celebratory hug at one point, according to fan footage shared on social media.

And while Swift has been known to bring her celebrity pals to Chiefs games, including Tom Cruise and Caitlin Clark to name a few, her spending time with Kloss is particularly notable as they were rumored to have grown apart after being best friends in the mid 2010s.

Speculation surrounding their friendship began after the former Victoria’s Secret Angel’s name was noticeably left off a T-shirt that Swift wore in her 2017 music video for “Look What You Made Me Do”, which featured a list of her girl squad.

And though Kloss attempted to calm down the speculation by sharing a photo with Swift backstage at the Reputation tour in 2018, the “I Knew It, I Knew You” singer did not attend Kloss’ wedding to Kushner—with whom she also shares kids Elijah, 3, and Rae, 13 months—a few months later.

But the two seemingly confirmed that any past bad blood had been washed away when Kloss and her husband attended Swift and Kelce’s white veiled nuptials at New York City’s Madison Square Garden in July.

And just a few weeks after the star-studded occasion, Kloss appeared to prove all was well while shedding light on Swift’s special day.

For a closer look at Swift being a cheer captain at Chiefs games, keep reading...

While supporting Travis Kelce as the Kansas City Chiefs faced off against the Chicago Bears on Sept. 24, 2023, her first-ever NFL game at Arrowhead Stadium, Taylor Swift sported DÔEN's white Lois Tank and Ksubi's distressed denim shorts, which she paired with a Chiefs windbreaker and matching New Balance sneakers.

For the Chiefs' Oct. 1, 2023 game against the New York Jets, held at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, Swift wore Area denim shorts, which quickly sold out. The singer completed the look with Christian Louboutin boots and a relaxed leather shirt from Gant.

Of course, Swift didn't forget her signature red lip for the star-studded game, which was also attended by Blake Lively and Ryan Reynolds.

#826. On this day in space! Nov. 5, 2002: NASA's Galileo spacecraft flies by Jupiter moon Amalthea only to find it's a 'pile of icy rubble less dense than water'

The Galileo spacecraft was running on cosmic fumes by the time it reached Amalthea and the flyby would be a last of its kind.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 5, 2002, NASA's old Galileo spacecraft was almost out of fuel. But the Jupiter mission still had some science to do. Galileo flew by a small moon called Amalthea. Amalthea is small, but it's interesting for scientists.

The Jupiter moon Amalthea is the reddest object in our solar system. It also generates more heat than it gets from the sun. Scientists think Amalthea creates electrical currents as it orbits in Jupiter's huge magnetic field. Near this little moon, strong radiation from Jupiter is dangerous for spacecraft.

The flyby caused some problems for Galileo. The spacecraft went into safe mode only 30 minutes after going past Amalthea. NASA said it was ready for problems, because Galileo was on its last legs, and the radiation near Amalthea was strong. However, NASA quickly fixed the problem and got Galileo working again.

Less than a year later, Galileo threw itself into Jupiter's atmosphere. The spacecraft was crushed by the high pressure in Jupiter's atmosphere, but its data still survives on Earth.

The Galileo spacecraft was running on cosmic fumes by the time it reached Amalthea and the flyby would be the last time the probe would ever swing by one of Jupiter's moons.

While it may not look like it in Galileo's black and white images above and below, Amalthea is tinted red due sulfur contamination on its surface. The moon is small, about 168 miles long, and orbits about 112,468 miles (181,000 km) from Jupiter (much closer to the planet than the Earth and its moon).

Galileo flew within 99 miles of Amalthea during its flyby, which also marked the closest Galileo would get to Jupiter before its death dive in September 2005.

"Scientists studying data from NASA's Galileo spacecraft have found that Jupiter's moon Amalthea is a pile of icy rubble less dense than water," NASA announced in May 2005

"Amalthea is throwing us a curve ball," Torrence Johnson, a study co-author on the Almathea flyby and project scientist for the Galileo mission at JPL, said in 2005. "Its density is well below that of water ice, and even with substantial porosity, Amalthea probably contains a lot of water ice, as well as rock."

Originally known as Jupiter V (because it was the fifth Jupiter moon discovered after the so-called Galilean moons Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto), Amalthea was named after naiad, or water nymph, from Greek mythology.

It is fitting that Amalthea was the last of Jupiter's moons to be visited by the Galileo spacecraft. The moon was also last Jupiter moon to be discovered by visual observations when it was first disovered by astronomer Edward Emerson Barnard in September 1892 using the Lick Observatory telescope in California.

The Galileo spacecraft ultimately crashed into Jupiter on Sept. 21, 2005, less than a year after its Amalthea flyby.

After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. #825. Berkhamsted players banned from watching FA Cup draw

Chris Devane says his players will be banned from the "distraction" of the FA Cup second round draw

The manager of seventh-tier Berkhamsted says his players have been banned from the "distraction" of the FA Cup second round draw.

The Hertfordshire club travel to fellow Southern League Premier Division South side Plymouth Parkway in the final tie of the first round on Monday, with the draw to be made ahead of the 19:30 kick-off.

The tie will be broadcast to an international television audience, and, like their hosts, Berkhamsted have never previously reached this stage of the competition.

"I've told the players they're not allowed anywhere near it [the draw]. Someone could tell me if they want who we get. I'm not really bothered about it," said Comrades boss Chris Devane.

Plymouth Parkway players dream of glamorous FA Cup tie

"It's important the players are focused on what they're there to do and that's win a football game. There's no point losing focus about who you may play if you do win, if you end up jeopardising the opportunity to win by doing so.

"The players will be nowhere near it. I've told them all, let me deal with all the press, let me deal with the TV interviews. You guys have got a job to do. Let me worry about sweeping the floor, so to speak, so that's what the plan is."

Berkhamsted, formed in 2009 after Berkhamsted Town folded, have beaten Bishop's Stortford, Hendon, Redditch United and Southend United to reach this stage - winning Â£20,625 from the FA's prize fund in the process.

The winners of Monday's tie will take Â£47,750, with Â£15,800 going to the losers. Both clubs will also pocket Â£50,000 for the tie being selected for broadcast.

The Comrades travelled down to Devon on Sunday, with their part-time players due to return home on Tuesday - and many needing to take unpaid leave from work.

Speaking to BBC Three Counties Radio, Devane said: "I'm really intrigued to see how much will a proper day of rest, prep and pre-match meal actually helps them [my players]."

Berkhamsted are featuring in the FA Cup first round for the first time in their history

#823. That’s a Mora: Rodrigo and Roma rise with Lazio to give Eternal City new life

Roma and Lazio have both made unbeaten starts to the Serie A season, giving those in the Italian capital dreams of a Scudetto

After nine games in 28 days, Gian Piero Gasperini finally got a moment to pause and reflect on Sunday night. The Roma manager was back in Liguria, where he worked for the best part of a decade across two stints at Genoa, to collect an award from Stelle Nello Sport – an association formed to promote sport in the region – celebrating his career achievements and commitment to courageous attacking football.

The timing worked out well. Gasperini’s Roma thumped Sassuolo 3-0 on Saturday, bouncing back from a midweek loss to Manchester United. That result meant the Giallorossi had scored 31 times in 11 Serie A games. In the last 65 years only two Italian teams – the Juventus and Napoli sides of 2017-18 – had ever made a more prolific start to a top-flight campaign. More importantly, Roma’s victory meant they remained undefeated in domestic competition this season. Just like their neighbours Lazio, who drew 1-1 away to Napoli in Sunday’s early kick-off.

Roma Caput Mundi? The old Latin phrase positions Rome as the capital of the world. Probably a little bit of a stretch, given Roma’s result against United. Lazio are not even competing in European competition this season and their own manager, Gennaro Gattuso, keeps claiming his priority is to avoid relegation.

Still, this is an extraordinary moment for football in the capital. According to Opta, this is the first time two teams from the same city have ever made it through 11 games of a Serie A season without a single defeat. When you consider that Rome’s two leading clubs have won just five Scudetti between them – as compared to 40 combined for Internazionale and Milan – the statistic jumps out even more.

Acknowledging this detail in an interview after collecting his award, Gasperini could not help but draw a contrast between his team and their rivals. “It’s a bit of a surprise for everyone to have this Scudetto derby situation playing out in November,” he said. “But it’s a reflection of the values of the city. “Rome is an extraordinary city which has a huge enthusiasm for football. For Roma the stadium is always full. Lazio might have some other problems. But the passion for football in Rome is incredible.”

His reference was to the mass boycott of Lazio’s home games by supporters, the reasons for which have been covered in recent editions of this column. Attendance figures for the Biancocelesti’s home games at the Stadio Olimpico this season hover at about 10,000 people. Roma drew 64,674 for Sassuolo on Saturday – in line with their average. Ticket sales do not decide football games. Lazio sit top of the table heading into the international break. But Roma have plenty to feel good about too.

Sassuolo were about the best team they could have faced this weekend. Seeking a bounce-back after their collapse in Manchester, Roma lined up against opponents who had earned a single point from their previous six games and owned the leakiest defence in the division.

Leonardo Balerdi had a header cleared off the line before Mario Hermoso put Roma ahead in the 27th minute, punishing some indecisive defending. Moments later, a scuffed shot from Donyell Malen – bobbling far off target – took deviations off a pair of Sassuolo players and wound up in the back of the net. The only question left was how many goals Roma would add. In the end it was just one, Rodrigo Mora cutting in from the left and swapping passes with Malen before striking back across his body into the bottom corner from the right side of the box.

A third consecutive Serie A game with a goal for the 19-year-old, who also set up Matías Soulé’s opener against United. And the Portuguese even played the initial ball to create the chance that led to their penalty in that game as well.

Gasperini has never been shy in his enthusiasm for Mora. “We’re standing before an extraordinary talent,” said the manager after including the teenager in his starting XI for a season-opening 4-0 win over Fiorentina in August. “Every time he touches the ball something beautiful happens.”

is not alone in noticing. Mora was called up by Portugal this week for their Nations League games against Denmark and Wales. He has trained with the senior team before but not played for them. There will be greater opportunities to do so now Cristiano Ronaldo has retired from international football, though Mora expressed regret, too, at not getting to train again with a man he described as “my idol”.

Back at Roma, Gasperini has tried not to ask too much, too soon, of Mora, giving him a full 90 minutes only once, in a Champions League rout of Slovan Bratislava. Otherwise, he has alternated starts with opportunities from the bench during this busy early-season stretch.

Only in the last week did that change. Mora started against Udinese, scoring the second goal in a 5-2 win, then was back in the lineup to face United. Gasperini’s decision to take him off at half-time of that game has been widely criticised. These things are always easy to oversimplify, but it is true that Roma’s attacking threat seemed to vanish with Mora missing after the interval.

Venezia 2-1 Udinese, Torino 1-1 Lecce, Cagliari 1-0 Frosinone, Parma 1-2 Bologna, Roma 3-0 Sassuolo, Napoli 1-1 Lazio, Monza 0-1 Atalanta, Genoa 1-2 Milan, Inter 2-0 Como, Fiorentina 2-2 Juventus

Gasperini spoke at the end of that defeat of it being a lesson that Roma could learn from. His team is still a work in progress, but the trend lines are more than encouraging. Roma secured their Champions League spot by winning six of their final seven games last season. They have not lost a domestic home game for more than 11 months and even their most recent away defeat in Serie A, to Inter, was all the way back in April.

Mora’s rapid ascent has added a new wrinkle. The attack we have seen in Roma’s last three games, with him and Soulé playing either side of Malen in a 3-4-2-1 has carved opponents open with such devastating effectiveness that you could start to wonder whether a healthy Paulo Dybala – for so long the standout talent here – would displace any of them from a first-choice XI.

This is not really a debate anyone needs to have. Roma hope to get Dybala back from his calf injury after the international round, but his body has always imposed breaks for him in every season and the Giallorossi will need rotation in any case to keep everyone fresh through a long campaign.

The improved depth of Roma’s squad, on the other hand, is a reason to believe that they can sustain their strong start. Gasperini, like most managers, would prefer to talk about the next game than discuss title ambitions this early in a campaign, but when a reporter asked if he would sign up now for a guaranteed second place he dismissed the idea out of hand.

“We don’t need to give ourselves false illusions, but we’re not going to knock ourselves down for no reason either,” he said. “I don’t know what we can achieve.”

#822. Musiala may never return to his best - Hoeness

Jamal Musiala has won 46 caps for Germany

Bayern Munich forward Jamal Musiala may never "regain the performance level he once had", says honorary president Uli Hoeness.

The 23-year-old Germany international collapsed twice in four days during pre-season and it was later revealed he had a treatable "neurological dysfunction".

Musiala has scored two goals in four games for Bayern in all competitions this season.

"We are facing a dilemma in this case, as he is suffering from an illness that cannot simply be cured, but it can be controlled to a certain extent with the use of medication," Hoeness told Bavarian network BR24.

Hoeness said Bayern would support Musiala, who is under contract until 2030.

Former Bayern and Germany captain Lothar Matthaus said Hoeness is trying to motivate Musiala.

"He's needling him a little. It's not just about wrapping him in cotton wool. He also has to battle against adversity sometimes," Matthaus told Sky90.

"Uli was looking to create that adversity with this statement.

"It's fine for him to say something like that, because we can't just put a positive spin on things and somehow wait for him to come back.

"If I were in Jamal Musiala's position, that would be motivation enough to show Uli I'm back."

Musiala joined Bayern in 2019 after coming through Chelsea's academy.

He has scored 71 goals and provided 38 assists in 235 matches for Bayern since breaking into the team as a 17-year-old.

One of the youngest Germany players in history, Musiala shared the Golden Boot as the joint leading scorer at Euro 2024.

He has not played for Bayern since suffering a hamstring injury in September, but recently returned to training.
