#821. Maya Jama Steps Down As Love Island UK Host After 9 Seasons

Love Island UK host Maya Jama announced she’s exiting the dating reality series after nine seasons, sharing the news in a lengthy statement: “All good things must come to an end.”

The most iconic bombshell is leaving the Villa.

Love Island UK host Maya Jama revealed she’s decided not to return to the dating series after nine seasons, reflecting on her journey on the ITV reality show in a heartfelt statement.

“What an incredible era and what an unforgettable time I’ve had, it’s been far too much fun to put into words or a video,” the British TV presenter wrote in a Nov. 8 Instagram post, “but as all good things must come to an end, it’s my time to step down as the host of my beloved Love Island.”

Alongside a video compilation of memorable moments over the years, Jama—who served as host on the ITV series and the companion show Love Island Aftersun, along with spinoffs Love Island Games and Love Island: All-Stars—expressed her gratitude toward those who supported her throughout her experience.

“I want to thank all of the people who rooted so hard for me to host the show in the first place. I wouldn’t change a thing,” she wrote. “To the fans of the show, thank you for every supportive message and every single time you’ve tuned in during my time as host, I’m forever grateful to you all.”

Jama added, “The show really does belong to the people who watch it and embrace it year after year.”

After thanking the “incredible production team,” the 32-year-old—who took over hosting duties in 2023 after Laura Whitmore’s exit—shared insight into her years with the “iconic” reality TV show franchise.

“I started hosting the show aged 28 and during the 9 incredible series met the most wonderful humans along the way,” Jama recalled. “I’ve loved every slow-mo walk, fire pit and live show. I’ll forever be grateful for the experience.”

While the Celebrity Traitors star didn’t go into detail about her decision to step away from Love Island, she gave a glimpse at her mindset.

“I’ve always believed that to truly grow, you have to take a leap every now and then,” she wrote, “and now is my time to throw myself into something new.”

Jama concluded her goodbye message with a touching sentiment, emphasizing that she’ll continue to be a fan.

“While my own Love Island journey has come to an end,” she wrote, “I wish the show and the team all the success in the world, I’ll be cheering you lot on from the sidelines forever.”

The Gentlemen actress summarized her thoughts while reposting her Reel on her Instagram Stories, writing, “I feel emotional,” adding that it's an “end of an era.”

For a closer look at more stars who departed their hit TV shows, keep reading…

Gregg Sulkin, Wizards Beyond Waverly Place

In the Wizards of Waverly Place spinoff's shocking series finale, Selena Gomez's Alex Russo reunited with teen love Mason Greyback (Sulkin)—only to reveal a devastating twist.

Greyback revealed his character died during the August 2026 episode, then his ghost filled in the gaps on what Alex has been up to in the years since his passing.

"You have a whole other life, Alex," he told her. "You got married. You have a beautiful daughter. And she needs you. That’s the life that you’re meant to live. You have to go back."

The couple announced that the third season of The Valley will be their last following a tumultuous season during which Danny’s drinking habits were questioned and he was accused of acting inappropriately while drinking.

“We’re incredibly grateful for this experience,” Danny and Nia—who share son Asher, 4, twins Isabelle and Zariah, 3, and Adelaide, 15 months—wrote in their September 2026 statement shared to social media, “but our priority is protecting our peace and our family. We are fully committed to each other and our beautiful children.”

The OneChicago fanbase was shocked when news broke in July 2026 that Miñoso, who has portrayed firefighter Joe Cruz since the show debuted in 2012, would be leaving the NBC drama during its upcoming 15th season.

The world of fire and ice featured another gruesome casualty as Ser Criston Cole was killed in the Riverlands during the Game of Thrones spinoff's July 26, 2026, episode.

In July 2026, E! News learned that Hawkins—who has portrayed Officer Kevin Atwater since the NBC drama debuted in 2014—was leaving the show after 13 seasons.

The "It's Not Unusual" singer claimed he was fired from his coaching position after 13 seasons over "financial difficulty with insurance."

“To be clear, I did not want to leave The Voice as l love the show and really appreciate the audience. ITV made this decision—obviously a while ago, and I was told just recently," Jones wrote on Instagram in September 2026. "They are offering a much-reduced role where I would make an appearance but without being actually involved from the start, and I’m not thrilled about that."

E! News confirmed in July 2026 that Scott—who has portrayed Detective Vincent Riley since the the long-running NBC crime drama's 23rd season—would leave during show's upcoming 26th season.

The Paramount+ drama's season 19 finale, released July 23, confirmed the longtime star will not be returning for season 20 after his character Elias Voit was locked up in prison for a murder he took the blame for.

"It was hard to say goodbye," Gilford told Us Weekly of his exit. "It definitely was one of my favorite characters I’ve ever gotten to play and partially because what a gift. Every season I got to do a different side of this character. It wasn’t like I was just doing the same thing every year."

Days after West Wilson confirmed his Summer House exit, news broke that Amanda, who has been a main cast member of the Bravo series since season two, will also not be returning for season 11 amid the fallout from their bombshell romance.

After his secret love affair with Amanda Batula nearly destroyed the cast friend group dynamic following season 10, it was no shocker that West walked away from the scandal (and the series) in June 2026 just weeks before season 11 was set to start filming.

The Rookie's corrupt lawyer Monica Stevens was no novice when it came to escaping death. "She's escaped multiple assassinations," actress Bridget Regan recounted to TV Insider of her character's four-season journey, "and prison time and being thrown in a woodchipper."

So when the attorney met her end on an April 2026 episode, "I wasn’t surprised," Regan noted. "I thought, 'Fair enough.' She’s had an amazing run, four years on this show. I’m only filled with gratitude."

Whitney Leavitt, The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives

After making her big break on Dancing With the Stars and landing a starring role in Chicago and Broadway, the Utah native announced season five of the hit Hulu reality show will be her last as she's moving on to other professional projects.

Dr. Samira Mohan is checking out of The Pitt. Actress Supriya Ganesh will not be returning for season three of the HBO Max drama, Variety reported in April.

The exit isn't so shocking to fans given that Ganesh's character has been planning to take on a new residency program at another medical center.

The crime procedural said goodbye to Director Leon Vance (played by Rocky Carroll) in a March 2026 episode, 18 years after the leader's debut in season five. During the 500th episode, Vance was killed in a shooting with a corrupt agent and welcomed to heaven by late Chief Medical Examiner Donald "Ducky" Mallard (played by Adam Campbell).

Mehcad Brooks shocked fans in 2025 when it was revealed he was leaving the NBC crime drama ahead of season 25.

Brooks, who joined the show in 2022, portrayed Detective Jalen Shaw for three seasons.

Kevin McKidd and Kim Raver, who have played Dr. Owen Hunt and Dr. Teddy Altman respectively for nearly 20 years, shocked fans with news that they are leaving the medical drama, with their final episode being the season 22 finale May 7, 2026.

Jenna Lyons, The Real Housewives of New York City

Jenna Lyons announced she will not be returning for The Real Housewives of New York City's 16th season.

"The rumors …..Are true," the former J. Crew Creative Director wrote on Instagram in November 2025. "I was grateful to be asked to join season 16 of RHONY 'as a friend of '- knowing my personal life was not really available to be filmed, we agreed that made sense."

The fashion icon—who joined the Bravo series for season 14 in 2022—explained that she later realized being a supporting castmember wasn't for her.

"And after thinking it through I have made the difficult decision not return to the show," she continued. "I would be the oldest and only openly gay woman on the show and feel like this is an opportunity for a new dynamic to emerge."

After nine seasons, the A-list realtor is done selling mega-mansions on the Netflix reality show.

“I’ve gotten to a place where I don’t need the show financially,” Chrishell announed in November via social media. “I’m lucky to have other forms of employment, because it’s no longer good for my mental health.”

Jax Taylor announced he will not be returning to The Valley for season three amid growing concern from fans about his behavior during the show’s second season.

“Right now, my focus needs to be on my sobriety, my mental health, and coparenting," the Bravo star—who is embroiled in a nasty divorce from estranged wife Brittany Cartwright—shared in July 2025. "Taking this time is necessary for me to become the best version of myself—especially for our son, Cruz.”

Michael Longfellow, Emil Wakim & Devon Walker, Saturday Night Live

The Saturday Night Live stars all announced within days of each other that they would not be returning for the sketch comedy series' 51st season.

Longfellow and Walker each spent three seasons on SNL while Wakim exited after just one season.

Heidi Gardner & Ego Nwodim, Saturday Night Live

Weeks after Longfellow, Walker and Wakim left SNL, longtime fan-favorites Gardner and Nwodim also confirmed they would not be returning for season 51 after eight and seven seasons, respectively.

Sofia Mattsson exited the long-running soap opera in summer 2025 after seven years playing Sasha Gilmore. Her character left Port Charles for Paris.

The Pitt star Tracy Ifeachor walked away from the hit HBO Max series after the medical drama's breakout first season.

"It was an absolute privilege to play Dr. Heather Collins in such a groundbreaking season and piece," the actress posted on Instagram July 10. "Thank you to everyone who has watched & supported Season 1 & shared their stories with me."

While fans maybe should have been aware that the days were numbered for Pedro Pascal's Joel Miller, considering his April 2025 death was quite similar to how it unfolded in The Last of Us Part II, the 2020 video game season two of The Last of Us is based on, the moment his character was brutally impaled still stunned.

Pascal, meanwhile, who also died onscreen in Game of Thrones and Buffy the Vampire Slayer, took his game over status in stride. "I get killed a lot," he joked to Entertainment Weekly. "I like to die."

After what he dubbed "one wild adventure," Peter Krause officially extinguished his role as 9-1-1's Los Angeles Fire Department captain Bobby Nash on an April 2025 episode of the procedural drama.

“Bobby Nash was written in sacrifice, and he was built for this,” Krause wrote in a statement to the Hollywood Reporter. “First responders risk their lives on the job so that others can see another day. His story arc honors them.”

Killing off the somewhat tormented, but beloved, firefighter was certainly a hot topic, showrunner Tim Minear acknowledged to Variety, "but after eight years, it just felt like, if we have any hope of creating stories going forward that have actual stakes, then someone's got to die."

Paige DeSorbo announced in June 2025 that she was walking away from the Bravo series after seven seasons.

"You’ve seen me grow up over these last 7 summers. I’ll always be grateful for the memories, the community, and the opportunities this wild ride has brought me," the Giggly Squad podcast cohost shared with fans on Instagram. "But like all good things (and some bad decisions), it’s time for this chapter to close."

The French actress confirmed she would not return for the hit Netflix series' fifth season in April 2025.

"After an incredible journey, I’ve made the decision to step away from Emily in Paris,” she wrote in an April 23 Instagram post, alongside pictures of her and her former castmates on set. “It has been a truly wonderful experience, one filled with growth, creativity, and unforgettable memories.”

Ahead of The Sex Lives of College Girls' third season, Reneé Rapp announced she would be leaving the Max series.

"College Girls moved me out to LA and introduced me to some of my favorite people," she wrote on social media in July 2023. "2 and a half years later—it's given me y'all and this community."

The show's co-creator Mindy Kaling also confirmed Rapp's exit. "We love @reneerapp so much and of course will be so sad to say goodbye to Leighton Murray!" Kaling wrote on her Instagram Stories before referencing Rapp's thriving music career. "We can't wait to see our friend on tour!!"

More than a year after Kevin Costner was rumored to have unexpectedly walked away from the hit Paramount drama after four and a half seasons, he confirmed in June 2024 that he will not return to finish out the series' fifth and final season.

After 19 years as Meredith Grey, Ellen Pompeo scrubbed in for the last time as a series regular on the ABC drama in February 2023.

"I gotta mix it up a little bit," Pompeo explained on The Drew Barrymore Show in December 2022, though she has already returned for a May guest appearance and continues narrating the series. "I'm 53, my brain is like scrambled eggs. I gotta do something new. You can't do The New York Times crossword puzzle every single day."

But she's not gone for good. Pompeo still pops in and out of Grey Sloan Memorial Hospital.

#820. Earth has captured a new mini moon  — but it won't stick around for long

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earth has caught itself a new mini-moon, and it is sticking around for Christmas.

The space rock, designated 2026 QQ8, was first observed in August 2026 after entering orbit around Earth in April 2026. The discovery was reported by the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center on Thursday (Oct. 29).

The stay of QQ8 is a temporary one. The mini-moon will remain in the thrall of Earth's gravity through December before breaking away in 2027.

Scientists have recreated the orbital path of QQ8, finding that it takes 359 days, or about 0.98 of an Earth year, to orbit the sun. QQ8 closely approaches Earth around once every ten years, but this time the object came so close that Earth has been able to gravitationally seize it.

According to the Minor Planet Center, the closest QQ8 will come to our planet during this stay is around 353,000 miles (568,000 kilometers). That is around 110,000 miles (177,000 km) further out than the average distance between Earth and the moon. Even if QQ8 were to come close enough to collide with Earth, it would likely be completely destroyed in our planet's atmosphere before it reaches the surface, as it is only around 6 feet (2 meters) in diameter.

This is far from the first time Earth has snagged itself a mini-moon, more accurately called a temporary satellite. In fact, research last year suggested that our planet could be orbited by as many as six mini-moons at any given time, with many of these being fragments of our more permanent natural satellite, the moon.

While QQ8 is tiny, it is larger than the average mini-moon. That is according to modelling earlier this year that suggested the average size for a temporary satellite is 75 centimeters (30 inches) across.

The same modelling suggested the average stay for such an object would be around nine months.

So if QQ8 was captured in April 2026, that means it should move away in January 2027.

The researchers behind those findings suggested that, were Earth to gravitationally grip a space rock around 10 feet (3 meters) wide, it could serve as a mini-moon for 10 to 20 years.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

#819. Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action

Delap’s talents resurface in style, Gómez delights Brighton with more fireworks, and hair-pulling confusion at Everton

It would have been very easy for Oliver Glasner to lose patience with Liam Delap. The forward is still only 23, yet the days when he was rattling in 12 in a Premier League season for Ipswich have come to seem a very long time ago (and his six games for Manchester City even longer). A season at Chelsea had left him bereft of confidence, an odd mix of diffidence and overaggression, devoid of composure in the box, arms flailing like a broken windmill. But the old gifts have not left him. Both goals on Saturday were the result of great muscular surges and if the first finish seemed essentially about hitting the ball as hard as possible on target, the second was a precise – and still powerful – finish in off the far post. After games such as this it’s possible to imagine him as England’s long-term replacement for Harry Kane. Jonathan Wilson

Match report: Nottingham Forest 3-1 Manchester City

Amid the chaotic blur of proceedings at Old Trafford, there was one outstanding performance. Alysson had only one goal to his name in his Premier League career at Aston Villa, but he scored one and helped set up another two in the first 48 minutes against Manchester United. The 20-year-old winger, who has represented Brazil only at under-16 level, was signed from Grêmio for an initial £8.7m last January. His only goal in 18 previous appearances was against Nottingham Forest in September – it took less than a minute to open the scoring at United and less than four for his saved shot to rebound out to Nicolas Jackson for Villa’s second. United’s right-back, Diogo Dalot, was too slow to close Alysson down for his opener and did not have any complaints when his trip on the Brazilian conceded a penalty at the start of the second half. Dalot, often the face of United’s struggles, was booed off when substituted in the second half – Alysson was applauded off by the away end. Billy Munday

Match report: Manchester United 4-4 Aston Villa

Diego Gómez is the latest example of a slow-burning Brighton player given the chance and space to bed in before then flourishing. His current status is as an overnight sensation, though a taste for the spectacular and an eye for goal have been obvious since two goals against Leeds in November 2025. Gómez had signed from Inter Miami that January. The inside-right position from which he drilled his left-foot sidewinder to open the scoring against Brentford brings the best from his shooting prowess with both feet. His October halfway line strike against Crystal Palace came with his right foot. As with a number of Brighton’s purchases, Gómez can play in other positions, variously defensive midfielder, attacking midfielder, even on the wing. Within Fabian Hürzeler’s stringent tactical setup, he is asked to work hard for the ball. Such high pressing created the opportunity Charalampos Kostoulas should have done better with in the moments after the opening goal. John Brewin

There is nothing wrong with Arsenal’s habit of winning games by a single goal: Mikel Arteta’s side did it 15 times on their way to the title last season and the latest against Hull was their fourth this season. Yet despite being six points clear of Manchester City heading into the international break, Arteta will have some concerns about the lack of goals so far. With only 15 from their first 10 matches, Arsenal are on course to break Manchester United’s record of 67 for the fewest by a team being crowned champions in 1993 – the Premier League’s first season. They have also been struggling to score in the first half of games, having gone six matches in all competitions without doing so last month, and Arteta has called on his players to be more ruthless. “Sometimes we try to score the perfect goal against low blocks, but we need to be much more chaotic than that. If we open the scoring much earlier also, it changes the game,” he said. Ed Aarons

All hail Brian Brobbey. It is fascinating that a player sometimes derided for his supposed lack of technical quality while at Ajax has developed into one of the Premier League’s most potent and difficult-to-play centre-forwards in little more than a year in England. His new contract, announced last Wednesday, is richly deserved. There is, as Régis Le Bris acknowledged after the win over Chelsea in which he bullied the visitors, no one quite like him. “Against a team that wants to press like that it’s so important to have a target man,” said the Sunderland manager, and Brobbey was that and then some. Much has been made of how Chelsea miss João Pedro but the Mackems are a different team with their flying Dutchman. Andy Brassell

It was a tale of two benches at Elland Road. The big question hanging over Leeds is whether they have the support for Dominic Calvert-Lewin to make a concerted push for Europe this season; a question that went some way to being answered when the substitutes Harry Wilson and Noah Okafor combined for the latter to score the winner against Tottenham. In contrast, Roberto De Zerbi’s attacking options let him down in a game that felt there for the taking. Dominic Solanke struggled after replacing Mathys Tel, Omar Marmoush looked limited in the central striker role and their brightest performer was the 18-year-old Lucá Williams-Barnett, who, you would suspect, is now not far from a deserved start. Having won three straight games before their defeat in West Yorkshire, Spurs suddenly go into the international break with more questions than answers over their attacking credentials once again. Aaron Bower

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Andoni Iraola had one wish as he signed off for the international window with the 3-1 win at Crystal Palace – that he does not lose any players to injury before Liverpool are back in action against Manchester United at Anfield on Sunday week. The manager is scarred by the previous round of international fixtures: Dominik Szoboszlai, Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak all picked up problems. The trio were missed as Liverpool lost to Manchester City in the first game back. Szoboszlai’s injury was the most concerning: he was only able to return as a substitute in the defeat against Arsenal on 1 November and Iraola said after the win at Palace that the Hungary midfielder was not 100%, that a knee problem required management. “Let’s see if Dom can play with the national team or not,” Iraola said. “I know what I want! But I have to understand the national teams. Also I’m sure Dom will want to go. I’m not sure if it’s going to be fine.” David Hytner

Match report: Crystal Palace 1-3 Liverpool

Bournemouth are really getting to grips with the Thursday-Sunday grind in their first season in Europe. Marco Rose has been working hard to ensure his team are in the right shape to start Premier League games quickly after a Europa League assignment three days earlier. After Thursday’s trip to face Sparta Prague, Bournemouth were quick out of the traps at Ipswich on Sunday, taking the lead through Evanilson after five minutes. “Last week [against Leeds] I said we start slow and this week we start quite quick and score an early goal – I am a magician,” said the head coach, after their eighth consecutive win in all competitions. That equalled a club record set under Eddie Howe in League One. Evanilson is himself on a streak – he’s scored in five in a row in the league – and only Nicolas Jackson has scored as many in the top flight since the last international break. The Brazilian did not need Christian Walton’s helping hand with this goal. BM

Newcastle delivered one of their more convincing performances of the season at Fulham, but one area remains a headache for Matthias Jaissle. Efforts to replace Alexander Isak in attack have not been good enough. Nick Woltemade was loaned to Juventus after an inconsistent debut season in England and there was not much encouragement to take from how Yoane Wissa and William Osula played at Craven Cottage. Wissa, who has struggled since his £55m move from Brentford last summer, has four goals in 41 appearances and did not put himself about enough before being taken off after 61 minutes, while Osula did not manage a touch in Fulham’s area and lost possession before Rodrigo Muniz’s late equaliser for the hosts. Jaissle needs more from his forwards on and off the ball. Otherwise Newcastle are going to need to find different players to lead their attack. Jacob Steinberg

The laws on hair-pulling were changed for this season after the red cards that were issued to Michael Keane, Lisandro Martínez and Dan Ballard in 2025-26. They are undoubtedly an improvement but, as James Tarkowski’s pull on Caleb Yirenkyi’s hair demonstrated in Everton’s comeback against Coventry, grey areas remain. Frank Lampard and David Moyes agreed the Everton captain should not have been sent off as there was no excessive force involved. But was it “a clear action without excessive force” that should have resulted in a yellow card for unsporting behaviour and a penalty to Coventry? Or “negligible, accidental or inadvertent contact” that is not usually considered an offence? Moyes offered up one solution – scrap the law altogether. “I think it is still ridiculous that is even categorised in the rules of the game,” the Everton manager said. “I can’t understand why they don’t fix this completely because I don’t see it as a good rule at all.” Andy Hunter

#818. Dutch match postponed after fans block team bus

Fans of Vitesse Arnhem celebrated an absence of away fans in the 2025-26 edition of their home match with De Graafschap

A Dutch second-tier match between Vitesse Arnhem and De Graafschap was called off after away team supporters blocked their own team's bus from departing for the game.

Fans of De Graafschap were protesting the decision to ban away fans from attending the game at Vitesse's GelreDome stadium after supporters had not agreed to security measures set out for the derby fixture.

Reports in Dutch media said De Graafschap fans gathered outside their stadium in Doetinchem early on Sunday and blocked the bus from leaving.

The Dutch Football Association said in a statement that the match would not go ahead on Sunday and that the matter would be referred to the disciplinary bodies.

"It is an unacceptable situation that the Vitesse - De Graafschap match cannot go ahead in this way. That supporters making football impossible is completely intolerable," it said.

"In doing so, they harm their club, their team, the sport, and the thousands of supporters who do come for the football."

In a Saturday statement, external, Vitesse announced that they had made the decision to ban away fans "based on police information and after extensive consultation with all involved security partners."

They had proposed an away fans allocation of 500 - cut from the standard 800 - dependent on a number of security measures including "fan paraphernalia brought along had to be subject to inspection prior to the supporters' arrival."

"Over the past few weeks, Vitesse, the police, and the municipality have repeatedly offered De Graafschap various options to meet these conditions.

"However, police information and conversations with De Graafschap indicate that a portion of the supporters is insisting on bringing fan paraphernalia in a manner contrary to the agreements made."

Vitesse added their decision had been made in light of "serious disturbances" surrounding the 2025-26 edition of the fixture, from which De Graafschap supporters were also banned.

In their response to the announcement, external, De Graafschap said they did "not recognize the picture painted by the Arnhem press release regarding the commitment and stance of our club and our supporters.

"As a club, we find it unacceptable that our supporters are portrayed in this manner."

Responding to the cancellation Vitesse director Willem van der Linden said the cancellation was a "major disappointment".

"A wonderful Gelderland derby between two regional clubs, in a well-filled stadium, could not go ahead today," he wrote in a letter posted on the club's website, external.

"In the run-up to the match, Vitesse, in close cooperation with all parties involved, did everything possible to still get the match started."

De Graafschap said in a statement on social media that they were "shocked by the incident" and "want to let the initial emotion subside and get a full picture of everything before we come with a further substantive response."

A new date for the fixture is yet to be announced, but Van der Linden said the intention was to hold the game "under the same circumstances."

Vitesse are 10th after the weekend's fixtures while De Graafschap, who play less than 20 miles to the east of their rivals, sit in 15th.

#817. WSL talking points: Tullis-Joyce takes charge and is Shaw the perfect striker?

The City striker hit a WSL hat-trick for the ninth time while Eva Olid’s United have found defensive stability

Not only did Khadija “Bunny” Shaw score a record-extending ninth WSL hat-trick, she scored a “perfect hat-trick” for the fourth time in the competition, something nobody else has managed more than once. Against West Ham the Jamaica striker opened the scoring with her left foot, headed home her second off the underside of the crossbar and tucked in her third with her right foot late on. It helped her side towards a 5-0 win that opened up a two-point gap at the top of the table and stretched Shaw’s lead in the race to be the top division’s top scorer to a five-goal advantage over her nearest challenger, Océane Hurtré. Can anybody stop her relentless pursuit of another Golden Boot? It would appear not. Tom Garry

Are Liverpool getting the points that their performances deserve? Arguably not, on Sunday’s showing. A 2-1 defeat against Arsenal left Gareth Taylor’s side just two places above the automatic relegation zone and just one spot above the relegation playoff place – despite creating plenty of chances and striking the crossbar, as they impressed in possession. Their defender Grace Fisk feels they are on the right path, saying: “Between both boxes I think we’re one of the best in the league, hands down. Sometimes, I’m watching the way our midfield is playing and the way they move, it’s just a joy to watch.” She added: “We gave it a good fight, I hope the fans see that, but it just wasn’t to be.” TG

London City Lionesses kept pace with Manchester City and Chelsea in the race for the WSL title ahead of a huge opportunity to gain ground next week. The Bromley-based side cruised to a 4-1 win against Birmingham on Sunday, keeping them third while moving them four points behind Chelsea, who face the leaders and title rivals City next week. One or both of the two leading sides will drop points at Stamford Bridge, allowing London City to gain ground in the race – if they beat struggling Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium. On the prospect of closing in on their rivals, the Lionesses head coach, Eder Maestre, said: “First we need to have a good result against Arsenal. The Emirates is going to be a very challenging environment so hopefully we can have a very good result and close the gap.” Emillia Hawkins

Manchester United may have a negative goal difference, having scored 10 and conceded 11 in nine WSL games, but they seem to have found the defensive solidity they were missing at the start of the season. Eight of those 11 goals conceded came in their opening three games as Eva Olid’s side adapted to the tactical demands and style of the new manager. “At the start, we didn’t have time together, just three or four weeks, and now we have more time together, I can feel the team improving,” the manager said after the 1-0 win over Aston Villa. “Still a lot of things to keep working on, not everything is perfect, but it’s good to see the way how things are progressing.” The Red Devils have kept three clean sheets in their past five WSL games and against Villa the backline and goalkeeper Phallon Tullis-Joyce were critical. “The opposition had two big chances and Phallon always helps,” said Olid. “I think that we need more confidence. I feel that the confidence is still a little low and it’s something we need to dedicate a lot of time to improve.” Suzanne Wrack

The result may have been crushing for Charlton, who are still yet to pick up a point in the WSL, but there were rare positives for Karen Hills to take from their 3-2 loss to Crystal Palace. It was the first time they had scored twice in a game this campaign and they accrued twice as many shots on target, six to three, than the home side. “At the end of the day, we’re all in this together. We’re all learning,” said Hills after Bethany England’s 90th-minute winner. “We’re all in a new league, playing against new opposition. But we knew Crystal Palace, we know them really, really well, and that game today was us. We played like a Charlton team does and I thought the performance deserved more.” Charlton have proved they can score at this level. Now they need better defensive performances if they are to earn their first points. SW

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

WSL roundup: Crystal Palace deny Charlton first point, London City stay third

Everton put on a display of defensive mettle as they thwarted Chelsea to earn a valuable point at Stamford Bridge. It was a performance that illustrated why they have the joint-second meanest defence in the WSL. The partnership of Naomi Layzell and Rion Ishikawa in the centre of the backline looked resilient once again, making a combined 29 defensive contributions. Layzell herself dominated in the box, making 14 clearances. Full-backs Hannah Blundell and Hikaru Kitagawa were crucial in nullifying the threat posed by Sandy Baltimore and Ellie Carpenter in wide areas. The latter, in particular, has been crucial to Chelsea’s attack this campaign with five goal involvements but was registered just one opportunity on Saturday. The home side, in general, were restricted to chances from set pieces. While creating 20 opportunities on goal, they had an xG of just 0.51 from open play, a clear indicator of how Everton were able to frustrate them. Sophie Downey

Olivia Holdt made her mark for Tottenham Hotspur once again as she put in an eye-catching performance in their 2-1 win over Brighton. With a goal and an assist, the 25-year-old creator proved crucial to Spurs’ ability to complete a second-half comeback. Her impact on their attack was clear to see. Starting on the left, she topped the stats for most touches in the opposition box (10) and most shots taken (4) and proved dangerous whenever in possession of the ball. Her relationship with fellow midfielder Signe Gaupset continues to develop, with Holdt setting up the Norwegian for the equaliser. This was the third consecutive game in which both have scored with Spurs becoming increasingly reliant on the duo as a source of goals. In contrast, Brighton struggled to create. Despite taking an early lead, Arturo Ruiz’s side looked toothless up front, registering just one of their three opportunities on target. SD

#816. Nick Jonas Details What He "Resents" About His Diabetes

Nick Jonas shed light on his decades-long journey with type 1 diabetes, revealing what he’s “grateful” for yet “resents” about the disease—which he was diagnosed with in 2005—in an open letter.

Nick Jonas is sharing insight into his health.

More than two decades after he was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, the Jonas Brothers member detailed his complicated relationship with the disease in an open letter to his “old friend.”

“How long has it been? 21 years. 21 years, and you haven’t changed a bit,” Jonas wrote in the letter, which is a part of Dexcom’s A Letter to Diabetes initiative. “It’s funny how often we talk. Every few minutes, honestly. Staring at my phone to see where my glucose is. Reaching for my pump to bolus because I’m about to eat something with 17 carbs.”

“Those are just a couple of the hundreds of little decisions I make every week,” he continued. “Most people never notice them. But they add up to a real relationship, because that’s what diabetes is. It’s an ongoing conversation between your body, your mind, and your devices.”

The “Burnin’ Up” singer noted that there are days it feels like he and his condition are “on the same team,” while on others it seems like his diabetes is on a “solo mission.”

As Jonas—dad to daughter Malti, 4, with wife Priyanka Chopra—put it, “In a lot of ways, that’s what family is like. You rely on each other, you push each other, and you know they’ll always be there.”

But when the “A Little Bit Longer” artist was first diagnosed with diabetes in November 2005 at age 13, its “unpredictability threw” him for a loop.

“I’d built my whole life around this unrealistic structure and belief that I was in control,” he wrote. “You took that apart over the years, bit by bit. Part of me is grateful I learned that lesson. Part of me resents you for it. Full stop.”

Jonas then admitted, “There are days I wonder what life would feel like without you.”

That said, the Camp Rock star emphasized that being diagnosed with diabetes brought him something unexpected: a strong “community.”

“I always struggled to feel like I belonged anywhere,” Jonas recalled. “At school, I felt misunderstood. In most circles, for that matter. Through my childhood and youth, that was the theme. It wasn’t until I started talking openly about life with type 1, and meeting other people who were living it too, that I finally felt like I belonged somewhere.”

And while the “Jealous” singer “never wanted” to been painted as a “victim,” he continues to be open about his “truth” to help others feel “a little less alone.”

“I share my story for the 13-year-old who just got diagnosed and is lying in a hospital bed, scared to death,” Jonas noted. “I want them to be able to look up and see someone out there living their dreams while managing all of this, every single day.”

To see what other stars had to say about their journeys with diabetes, keep reading…

Nick Jonas can hit up the waffle house with an appetite and the know-how to manage his glucose levels.

The Jonas Brothers member has become one of the most high-profile stars with type 1 diabetes, with his diagnosis at 13 years old coming right before the sibling trio hit it big on the Disney Channel and with their 2006 debut album It's About Time.

Years later, Nick co-founded the nonprofit Beyond Type 1. Per its website, the organization “aims to change what it means to live with chronic illness” by “bridging the gap from diagnosis to cure, empowering people to live well today and funding a better tomorrow.”

Since his diagnosis, brothers Kevin and Joe have had Nick’s back as he monitors his health while keeping up with their rock-and-roll schedule.

“They’re incredibly supportive, and really help normalize it,” Nick explained to TODAY.com in 2023. “They understand that if I was irritable for an hour, that it’s probably because my glucose is high. And they give me grace, or make sure that if I’m starting to go low that I’ve got the juice I need or whatever at my disposal quickly.”

While a majority of people with type 1 diabetes are diagnosed in childhood, a stunned Lance Bass was in his 40s.

The *NSYNC singer detailed his diagnosis in a 2024 Instagram video, revealing he was previously misdiagnosed with type 2 diabetes, when in reality, he had developed type 1.5 diabetes.

Initially, "I had a difficult time getting my glucose levels under control, even though I made adjustments to my diet, my medications and my workout routine,” Lance said. “Things just weren't adding up.”

He now wears a Dexcom Continuous Glucose Monitor attached to his body. It takes readings of blood glucose levels every few minutes and sends alerts to a phone or receiver if it's changing rapidly so the person can potentially eat something carb-heavy if it's falling too fast or give themselves extra insulin if it's rising.

Meanwhile, Lance and husband Michael Turchin's twins, Alexander and Violet, 3, have taken an interest in his diabetes management routines as they play doctor at home.

"I'll show them the little needle that sticks out, and they just think it's fascinating," he said about his blood glucose monitor. “They're not scared of it at all. I explain over and over why I do this and what diabetes is, and you know, I don't know how much of that they're understanding. But you know, eventually they will."

Este Haim, seen above rocking her CGM while also rocking out onstage during a Haim concert alongside sisters Danielle Haim and Alana Haim, revealed how living with T1D has impacted her love life.

“I had a guy break up with me because I said that there was a possibility that our kid would have diabetes," she told British GQ in June 2025. "He was like, ‘Then why are we here?’ And I was like, ‘What?!'“

But it wasn’t the first time Haim endured disappointing reactions to her chronic illness, which she’s been navigating since her diagnosis at 14 years old.

“I was basically a social pariah for a very long time,” she told Beyond Type 1 in 2019. “You know, I was just the kid with diabetes in school that passes out and no one knows why and the girl with diabetes that smelled like orange juice all the time.”

Thankfully, like Nick Jonas, Este’s siblings have consistently shown up for her as she navigates tour life. “I’m lucky that I have Danielle and Alana to be my support," Haim said, "and when I am having a bad day, a bad week, a bad month, they’re always the first people to be like, ‘Dude we got you. Whatever you need. We’re going to get through this. Let’s get you a healthy meal. Let’s not have pizza after the show tonight. Let’s go get you something good so that you don’t wake up and your blood sugar is 350.’”

Bret Michaels has detailed the thorns poking out of his rosy career.

In a June 2025 Instagram post, the Poison frontman explained how living with type 1 diabetes might impact his tour schedule after a health scare.

“Unfortunately, the highs and lows of living with diabetes since I've been six years old occasionally just kick my butt,” Michaels wrote. “Last night, I went on stage and even added a song or two to the set to prove to myself & the fans that I could do it. At the end, my blood sugar walking off the stage was a real-life 39.”

Per the CDC, 70 mg / dL is considered low blood sugar for people with T1D—and severe low blood sugar begins at 54 mg / dL.

“I vow in the near future, I'm going to take that time needed,” he told fans. “And please forgive me if I have to move some of the shows around until I get this under control.

That’s not to say, Michaels hasn’t taken plenty of precautions along his decades-spanning career.

"I wake up and the first thing I do is check my constant glucose monitor," Michaels told People in 2024. "I take an injection and then the next thing I do is I get up and—good, bad or indifferent, no matter how I'm feeling—I get into a workout routine, and it helps to level the blood sugar out.”

He added, "And then I jump into the fun and the business of the day, and just try to take every day like that."

John Legend and Chrissy Teigen's son Miles

John Legend and Chrissy Teigen are proving to be extraordinary people when it comes to their son Miles' type 1 diagnosis.

The Cravings cookbook author detailed their shock upon discovering his T1D status on, after Miles was hospitalized for an unrelated health issue. “I've learned since then that this is how so many young children end up being diagnosed with type-1," she wrote on Instagram in July 2024, "going to the hospital for something completely different."

Teigen—also mom to Lunda, Esti and Wren—later shared how this inspired her to become an advocate with advanced screening for T1D. “I was blown away by the fact that not only did I not know that screening was an option when I first had children—I have four kids by the way—I didn’t hear about early screening at any point during any of my pregnancies,” she said at the Women’s Health Lab panel in May 2025. “It would’ve made an incredible amount of difference.”

The Dancing With the Stars pro shared her Type 1 diabetes diagnosis in May 2024, and has since been open about the strength she's earned through her experience.

“It’s a hard diagnosis and it takes a lot of time and just thinking out of your life, but I think it’s made me stronger and more mature,” she told Woman’s World in a July 2025 interview. “I’m able to handle conflict and hard things in my life better, because I go through the management and just the hard things that come with type one diabetes.”

Plus, she added, “It brings me so much motivation every day, because I want to be an inspiration to others. I want to be an inspiration to young people or anyone with [any] type of diabetes, so if it really gives me that motivation every day that I’m doing it for them and not just for myself.”

Hoda Kotb got some breaking news about her daughter Hope in 2023.

Yet, the former Today anchor waited until after she left the morning show full-time to reveal her youngest child was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes.

“Hope is fine for most of the day. There are just moments where you have to watch her," she told former cohosts Craig Melvin and Savannah Guthrie when returning to Studio 1A in May 2025. "I was totaling it up—five minutes at breakfast, five minutes at lunch, five minutes at dinner, sometimes overnight. Add that up, that's a half-hour.”

“So, for 23 and a half hours,” Kotb added. “She's every other kid. So, I try to remember that."

Kate Moss' model daughter Lila Moss celebrated the debut of some diabetes-chic accessories made for a groundbreaking Barbie.

A continuous glucose monitor and insulin pump are signature features of Mattel’s first-ever doll with type 1 diabetes. As the company noted in a July 2025 statement, its collaboration with Breakthrough T1D was "designed with inclusion and empathy at the core."

To celebrate the release, Mattel honored two type 1 diabetes ambassadors, Peloton instructor Robin Arzón and Moss, presenting them with their own one-of-a-kind dolls.

Upon the Barbie’s reveal, Moss wrote on Instagram, "This has been such a special project to be a part of, I hope this can encourage anyone living with Type 1 to not be afraid of wearing their pump proudly and that it helps to raise awareness on why we have them and what they do for us!"

#815. Fishlock retires after record-breaking career

Jess Fishlock won more caps and scored more goals for Wales than any other player, male or female

Wales legend Jess Fishlock's playing career is over, after Seattle Reign were beaten 1-0 by Gotham FC in the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) play-off quarter-finals.

The 39-year-old midfielder began her career with home town club Cardiff City in 2002. She played in eight different countries and collected Champions League winners medals with FFC Frankfurt and Olympique Lyonnais.

Fishlock retired from international football in October 2025 after scoring 48 times in 166 international appearances - both Wales records.

She won three NWSL Shields during a 14-season stint with Seattle but announced in April this season would be her last.

"I've loved it," said an emotional Fishlock, as she wiped away tears after losing to Gotham on Sunday.

"And the truth is I've loved that my last year was with this group, because they have just given me so much, and not just on the field."

Fishlock will now be part of Rhian Wilkinson's Wales coaching staff for December's two-leg World Cup play-off against Norway.

Wales face Denmark and Italy again on League A return

Wales in fight to retain rising female stars

Fishlock, who has previously held player-coach roles at Cardiff City Ladies and Melbourne Victory, joined Seattle for the inaugural NWSL season in 2013.

Reign finished eighth in this year's regular season table to claim the final play-off berth, and they pushed number one seed Gotham close in a game during which Fishlock left the field in the 74th minute.

"Two years ago I was just 'I can't work with these kids', as in I'm too old for it, but they have given me just so much joy," added Fishlock.

"And obviously the older ones, we've just had to rely on each other so much these last couple of years and it's created deeper relationships within what we've already been doing, and because of that I've seen so much growth on and off the field from this team.

"So even today I'm not upset that I'll never play football again - I'm ok with that, I've played enough - but I am devastated that I will not get to spend more time with this group because they will win."

Reign defender Sofia Huerta said it had been a privelege to play with Fishlock, who she described as the best player she had ever seen.

"She came into this league and it was so lucky to have her," said Huerta. "She put this league on the map.

"Playing with Jess has been my greatest honour. I've seen her be the best professional, such a good player, but the best thing about Jess is she's just such a good person."

Jess Fishlock was named the NWSL's Most Valuable Player (MVP) in 2021

Fishlock helped Wales' women qualify for their first major finals in 2025, becoming the oldest scorer at a Women's European Championship in the 4-1 defeat by France.

However, she said it would not be easy to pick out one memory as a snapshot of her career.

"I look back and there's just so much to think about, not only with Reign but with Wales," mused Fishlock.

"It would have to be one of those panorama snapshots because it's too difficult.

"All I know is what I'm most proud of deeply in my soul is that... I've stayed with Wales - that was difficult for 20 years, wouldn't do it any other way - stayed with the Reign for 14 years, wouldn't do it any other way.

"Because for me, when you win with your people - with the people that you've struggled with, the people that you've lost with, the people that you've failed with - when you win with your people, there is no better feeling in the world."

Former Wales captain Kath Morgan, who coached Fishlock from the age of nine, told BBC Radio Wales' Breakfast programme the midfielder is the best player to have to come out of Wales.

And while Fishlock played for Bristol Academy in the early years of the Women's Super League (WSL) - winning the league's player's player of the year award in 2012 - and had a spell on loan at Reading during Seattle's off-season in 2020, Morgan believes England's top-flight missed out on a generational talent.

"For me, the telling point is that Jess has played all over the world, and you have to be a good player to get away with that," said Morgan.

"The only thing I would say is that the WSL has massively missed out on Jess's presence, which for me is a little bit disappointing.

"I think it was probably the wrong time, and she'd already kind of decided that she was going to settle over in Seattle, and she was happy there... obviously we've got to respect that, but it's just a shame."

#814. Blue Origin announces 3rd stage for its powerful New Glenn rocket —and a new engine

Blue Origin's big rocket is getting a little bigger.

Jeff Bezos' company announced today (Nov. 5) that it has developed a third stage for its New Glenn rocket, which it says will make the powerful launcher more capable and flexible.

The stage, called the GS3, "enhances New Glenn's capabilities," Blue Origin said in a blog post today. "The third stage enables direct deployment of satellite constellations to GEO [geostationary orbit] and supports heavy-lift science and exploration missions to the moon and deep space."

New Glenn is a two-stage vehicle at the moment. Its reusable first stage is powered by seven of Blue Origin's BE-4 engines, and its second stage features two of the company's BE-3Us. The rocket stands 322 feet (98 meters) tall and can haul 14.3 tons (13 metric tons) to geostationary transfer orbit (GTO) and 50 tons (45 metric tons) to low Earth orbit (LEO).

These are the specs for the standard, or "7x2," version of New Glenn. Last year, Blue Origin announced that it's developing a super-heavy variant known as the 9x4, because it will feature nine first-stage BE-4s and four upper-stage BE-3Us. The 9x4 will be nearly 400 feet (122 m) tall, and it will be able to loft 15.4 tons (14 metric tons) to GTO and 77 tons (70 metric tons) to LEO, according to Blue Origin.

New Glenn has flown three times to date, each time in the 7x2 configuration. The rocket debuted in January 2025, then launched again in November 2025 and again on April 19 of this year.

Things didn't go according to plan on that latest mission. The rocket deployed AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird 7 communications satellite into the wrong orbit, and the spacecraft ended up being lost.

Another setback came just a month later: On May 28, New Glenn exploded on the pad during a routine engine test at Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. Blue Origin has been working ever since to rebuild the pad and get New Glenn ready for its fourth flight, which is expected to occur late this year.

We now know that Blue Origin has also been working on the GS3 while those repairs were underway. The new stage will be powered by one BE-7 engine, which the company developed for use on its Blue Moon spacecraft, one of the two private vehicles that NASA selected to be crewed lunar landers for its Artemis program. (The other is SpaceX's Starship.)

Blue Moon landing missions won't need to launch on GS3-equipped New Glenn rockets, according to Blue Origin. But the third stage "can support sustained operations around the moon," the company wrote in today's blog post. "By delivering significant payload mass directly to trans-lunar injection (TLI), GS3 enables faster transit times while preserving propellant for on-orbit operations."

And there's already demand for such services: Blue Origin also announced today that a government customer (which it did not name) has booked a GS3 mission to cislunar (Earth-moon) space, with launch targeted for 2028.

And the company dropped yet more news today — that it's working on a new first-stage engine, called Northstar.

Like Blue Origin's other booster engine, the BE-4, Northstar burns liquid oxygen and liquid methane propellant, a combination known as methalox. But the new engine is more powerful and less complex.

"Compared to the BE-4 engine, Northstar reduces mass by 30% and parts count by 50%, while increasing thrust from 640,000 to 715,000 pounds-force," Blue Origin said in a second blog post today. "Manufacturing advancements have also significantly shortened production timelines, enabling assembly in less than a day."

Northstar went from program approval to development testing in just 11 months, according to the company. But today's update did not say when the new engine will fly for the first time.

#813. Football comes together across Spain to honour Jesús de Miguel: ‘We’ve seen how fragile life is’

Across La Liga and beyond this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them

In the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very important,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. Without thought. We have a grand day before us.”

With that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Club, rivals from the north, and together they went out past the little shrine of Saint Fermin on to the field. They carried white lilies and all wore the same white shirts with a No 9 on the back, a black ribbon and the name of Jesús de Miguel, the Tenerife striker who died after a collision on the pitch five days earlier at the age of 30. At almost exactly the same time, 2,000km away to the west, Tenerife’s squad were walking out at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López in Santa Cruz. They did not have anyone alongside them, wore black suits not white shirts and did not have a game to play either, not this week.

Two days earlier Tenerife had been in Navahermosa, La Mancha, the tiny village their teammate’s family are from, carrying the coffin of the friend their captain called “our Demigol”. They were supposed to be in Granada on Saturday; instead, they were back on the island, in their home ground, to say goodbye and pay homage. Publicly, this time. Lilies had been laid on the pitch there too, a Tenerife shirt with them, and a stage built at one end. “We’ve seen how fragile life is,” the captain, Enric Gallego, said, offering words he said could never be enough, carrying the burden for all of them. “We think of the journeys, the wins, the losses, and hold on to those moments that seemed normal, but that now … a few days ago we shared that with you. To talk of you in the past tense is unfair. None of us are prepared to live what we’re living through.”

No one ever could be. Across Spain this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them. That, Budimir had told his teammates, was something they must think about but not think about too. The players’ union in which De Miguel had a role, a footballer there for others, had asked for the competition to stop. Respect demanded that it did, they said, requesting a judge intervene when the league did not hear them. But it had gone on. The only matches postponed were those involving Tenerife; Andorra, whose goalkeeper Jesús Owono had crashed into De Miguel; and Castellón, who he had taken to the second division, delivering them to segunda for the first time in 16 years and himself for the first time at all, aged 27.

On the eve of the game that opened this weekend’s fixtures, the Sevilla head coach, Luis García, said he thought they should wait. It was too soon, too raw, too theirs. His midfielder Giorgi Kochorashvili had missed training the day before: a former Castellón player, Kochorashvili had asked permission to go to the funeral, leaving early and returning late, his mind elsewhere. Of course he could, García had replied, “we are humans above all else”. And it was not just him. García had worked with Owono – “let’s not make two victims, we have had enough; he is in hell, for sure”, he had pleaded – and now he said: “If there’s a play that’s similar … what do I say to my goalkeeper?

“We need time,” García had said. “We need to reflect.”

Instead, they played. From Seville on Friday night to Madrid on Sunday, via stadiums everywhere. It was, some suggested, the best way to pay homage to De Miguel but no one truly knew. “We can’t ask him what he would have wanted,” José Mourinho said before Madrid went to Valencia and won 3-0, Tenerife’s flag flying at half-mast at Mestalla. He might not have wanted anything at all. “You never wanted any attention,” Gallego said, but this weekend he was on all their minds.

“Forever in our memories,” the league’s line read. At every game in the first and second divisions, the ritual was repeated. Teams came out together wearing the same white shirts bearing his name. Flowers were laid, a little uncomfortably, on the spot inside the centre circle where he had fallen and there was a minute’s silence, players and officials gathered around the wreath. As they stood before Cádiz-Oviedo, tears ran down the cheeks of the Tenerife-based referee Marta Huerta de Aza. On stadium screens, an image of De Miguel appeared. On television screens, a QR code did: a link to a crowdfunding campaign for the young family he left, set up by the former Tenerife player Fran Sol.

The games began and then, in the ninth minute or as near as the referee could manage, they paused again: the teams stopped, looking up to the screen, where a video of his best moments played out. It was not always an easy watch, and some preferred not to.

At Sevilla, where fans saw Antonio Puerta collapse on the pitch and pass away, applause still offered in the 16th minute every game, Kochorashvili stood by the bench, eyes lost somewhere his mind was not. At Espanyol, where in the 21st minute they applaud Dani Jarque, the captain who died during a pre-season and to whom Andrés Iniesta dedicated the winning goal at the 2010 World Cup final, Álex Calatrava and Álvaro González, teammates at Castellón and Tenerife respectively, looked about to break. In the ninth minute at the Metropolitano, the place was still rocking, the timing out of sync: Giuliano Simeone had just scored, so the referee Javier Alberola Rojas allowed a couple of minutes to pass, choosing his moment, Diego Simeone helping him impose silence on the stands when he finally stopped it. Then they started again, expected to carry on regardless.

In Pamplona, Alejandro Catena, who scored the late equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Athletic, raised an Osasuna shirt with De Miguel’s name and number on the back. Theirs was the game that felt most out of place, attention drawn from where it should have been, where it was. It would not be true to say that it did not matter, the Osasuna head coach, Jagoba Arrasate, admitting he had been carried along with it like everyone else, the calmness he thought they had found in the months out of the game soon abandoned again.

As they played, grateful for the grand day that they had before them, all the days they did, the tribute continued in Tenerife. The Heliodoro had filled early, access by every gate except eight and nine, engulfed by flowers and candles. De Miguel’s shirt lay on the turf where he had, lilies to one side, a spotlight on it. Another wreath occupied the bench. A giant shirt stretched across one end where the stage was, a lectern awaiting the speakers. A cross presided over it. Staff and players wore No 9 badges on their lapels. Supporters came in Tenerife shirts. And in the yellow shirts of rivals Las Palmas, whose president and captain Kirian, who had recovered after cancer, came. “This is the Canaries I want,” said Tenerife’s majority shareholder, Rayco García.

In the seats set up on the pitch, Tenerife’s players and De Miguel’s family sat, their eyes heavy. The archbishop, Eloy Alberto Santiago led a mass. The club’s president and majority shareholder spoke. He promised they would never allow María, De Miguel’s widow, to be alone. He also announced they would adopt Carla, his 14-month-old daughter, supporting her economically until she is 18. Gallego addressed her, football as family meaning something. “I hope one day you can look back and see who your dad was, be proud of him, not just for the footballer he was but the person: for his humility, his goodness,” he said.

Sniffing, his voice breaking, the captain paid homage to his teammate, his strike partner, his friend. The kind of person, he said, who did not seem to be there, and definitely did not demand that people notice he was, but always was. A man, he noted, so disinclined to put anyone out that when his car broke down he walked home from training rather than bother anyone for a lift. That, he insisted, might not seem like much, but it said much. “Today we don’t want to talk only of the player; we want to talk about you, Jesús, about the person that was behind the shirt,” he had begun. “Above any game, any team, what really remains is the person and the impact you leave. And you were a very special person.”

Gallego gave way to the archbishop, orations led by Tenerife staff, and as the act came to a close, difficult days ahead, the spotlight taken elsewhere, the drums began and the fans belted out a familiar tune, once more with more meaningful than ever before:

double quotation markWe have to sing with even more strength if you’re losing Even those who left us sing, from heaven This will never stop We will sing to eternity.”

Then Tenerife’s players departed. They have training on Monday and next week they play.
